Electrostatic charges in powders emerge through particle-particle and particle-surface collisions via triboelectrification during pneumatic conveyancing, posing a significant safety risk by triggering numerous past fires and dust explosions in industrial settings. We utilized monodisperse PMMA particles injected into a developed airflow stream traveling first through a PMMA pipe followed by a metallic duct section. Using a Faraday cup located at the metallic duct outlet to measure particle charge, our observations across diverse environmental conditions revealed an initial increase in electrostatic charge with rising humidity, which peaks and subsequently declines as humidity continues to increase.

This study addresses how to strategically utilize edge and cloud resources to enhance accuracy and latency using Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. We introduce an integrated edge-cloud hybrid framework for stream analysis, designed to perform low-latency inference on the edge and conduct capacity-intimate training on the cloud. We detail an efficient software implementation and optimal method for precisely and approximately decomposing two-qubit unitaries based on any prescribed set of XX-type discrete interactions and local gate choices. Through manipulating specific polyhedral regions within the space of canonical operations in these systems, we identify minimal collections of XX-type terms that maximally reduce expectation infidelity according to experimental error constraints. Additionally, for generating exact Haar-random two-qubit circuits, incorporating CX's quadratic and cubic roots in addition to CX improves precision infidelity estimations by approximately 31.4%, approaching the near-theoretical ceiling of roughly 36.9%, which is attained by incorporating all potential fractional CX applications directly.

Although contrastive learning has proven effective for high-level tasks, it remains less studied in low-level applications because direct adoption fails to capture the essential texture and context details required, which are lacking when using global visual representations suited for high levels. This paper introduces an innovative contrastive framework specifically designed for single image super-resolution. Our investigation addresses sample construction and feature embedding, aiming to improve upon existing methods that simply use low-quality versus ground truth image pairs as positive/negatives or rely entirely on pre-trained priors like VGG to generate embeddings. Instead, we develop a practical approach within the SISR context that generates abundant hard negative and positive examples in the frequency domain and employs a lightweight embedding network inherited from a discriminator; this design ensures it can be co-optimized alongside the main super-resimulation model, reducing dependence on separate pretrained pathways and enhancing generality across SISK tasks without sacrificing task-performability accuracy. Through comprehensive benchmark evaluations, we achieve notable gains in image reconstruction performance, demonstrating improvements reaching 0.28 dB beyond state-of-the-art approaches for super resolution.

With the rise of the digital economy, personal information is becoming akin to "crude oil" of the twenty-first century and growing increasingly valuable. Mirroring this trend, emerging data markets facilitate exchanges between providers and consumers to monetize high-quality personal information; however, the inherent privacy risks of data analytics often deter providers from participating. While differential privacy represents the industry standard for mitigating these risks, it can simultaneously reduce data utility. This paper presents a billing scheme and a corresponding mechanism designed to balance privacy safeguards with dataset quality. The proposed framework incentivizes providers to reveal their true privacy valuation and optimizes data consumer profits within budgetary limits. The study formally proves the mechanism's efficacy regarding these goals and further validates the findings through experimental evidence.

Electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) enables the robust coupling of optical signals with electronic spin quantum coherence. While conventionally studied using idealized atomic ensembles with three-level systems sharing a common excited state, this technique has been adapted for c-axis divacancy color centers in silicon carbide, a quantum material suitable for near-IR optics yet challenging for standard resonance applications. These difficulties arise from significant optical transition inhomogeneity across the ensemble and the existence of numerous ground-state levels, which can otherwise suppress excitation signals. However, through meticulous optimization of the measurement configuration, EIT is demonstrably established in this solid-state platform with excellent visibility. Comparisons between experimental outcomes and Lindblad-based models confirm the all-optical generation of inter-channel quantum coherence among distinct ground-state sublevels, suggesting promise for wireless (RF-free) quantum sensors. Furthermore, this study advances the fundamental comprehension of EIT in highly inhomogeneous multi-level systems, a framework broadly applicable to various defects within semiconductors.

Coronavirus disease, also known as COVID-19, is an infectious disease caused by the SARs-CoV-2 virus, the first case of which was confirmed in Wuhan, China, in late December 2019. Following this emergence, the outbreak rapidly spread globally, including Indonesia, leading the World Health Organization (WHO) to declare it a pandemic. To forecast the increasing number of COVID-19 cases, particularly in Indonesia, this study evaluated Deep Neural Network (DNN) approaches, focusing specifically on the Deep Transformer model capable of time-series prediction. During training under multiple scenarios, the research optimized the best performer by identifying superior hyperparameters, including prediction horizons and the number of features to utilize, alongside comparisons with legacy Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) architectures. Utilizing Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) for assessment, the Deep Transformer model achieved optimal performance when configured with Adamax, Pre-Layer Normalization, one-day ahead predictions, resulting in a MAPE of 18.83. Consequently, this optimized configuration outperformed the other tested deep learning models.

The goal is to suppress ghosting and artifacts caused by moving objects. The second contribution involves developing a specific framework for handling these recovered details, which are the primary focus of the paper's methodology and evaluation against existing baseline methods. Farmers employ pesticides to mitigate losses in agricultural output, with treatment effectiveness often assessed by analyzing treatment means and risk distributions via stochastic efficiency analysis based on certainty equivalents ranking a target function. A primary limitation of this approach is the need for robust observational data to achieve statistical significance, an issue frequently encountered in field trials where replication and sample sizes are constrained. Therefore, the purpose of our research involves presenting an adapted methodology utilizing simulation-based techniques combined with quantile regression to capture disease effects under conditions of limited trial count. As proof of concept, we implement these methods to examine strawberry disease management strategies across Florida.

This paper introduces both a methodological approach and a utility tool designed to assess Distributed Energy Resources (DER) placement on distribution circuits for managing voltages and power flows. Drawing on our earlier development of Phasor-Based Control (PBC), where DERs provide real and reactive power to meet specific voltage magnitude and phase angle targets, this study applies linearized power flow equations alongside integral controls to create a linear state space representation of the PBC on a three-phase, unbalanced network. Leveraging this model, the paper investigates whether specific inverter-based DER arrangements can achieve stable controller gain sets—a task for which both contability analysis and the traditional Lyapunov method prove inadequate, requiring a parameter space sampling strategy. Notably, this stability assessment relies solely on line impedance modeling and avoids the computational expense of full system simulations. Finally, by integrating this evaluation process into a publicly accessible visualization tool, the results display three procedural methods for analyzing diverse control configurations on the IEEE 123-bus feeder.

A quantum algorithm functions as a set of instructions for a quantum processor; unlike those on classical systems, their outcomes cannot be guaranteed with absolute certainty. A quantum search algorithm can be characterized as the rotation of state vectors within a Hilbert space. Through sequences of iterations, these vectors are uniformly rotated toward a target location. To achieve optimization, the algorithm requires precise parameters, including the count of target items relative to the total number of possible states. This study presents the successful execution of the IBM Corporation-developed fixed-point optimal quantum search algorithm using their IBMQ simulation environment. We applied single iterations of the algorithm across 2, 3, 4, and 5-qubit systems and verified result accuracy using histogram analysis.

String diagrams offer an effective visual system for conducting equational reasoning regarding morphisms in monoidal categories. Contrary to standard term rewriting, rewriting string diagrammatically facilitates more concise proof paths, as the graphical representation formally justifies equalities based on monoidal monadicities (structure).

Manually manipulating these diagrams, particularly extensive or complex ones, proves to be labor-intensive and susceptible to errors; however, this challenge can be alleviated by adopting automated tools like the Quantomatic proof assistant.

Despite the utility of concrete string diagram manipulation, reasoning about specific instances alone may prove insufficient for certain applications, particularly when addressing entire sets of (potentially infinite) string diagram families. Such endeavors reintroduce the difficulties associated with concrete manipulation while significantly increasing the risk of error due to the nuances in precisely modeling infinite family representations.

Consequently, the primary objective of this thesis is the conception of a mathematical framework designed for equational reasoning over infinite string diagram families that is specifically adaptable for computer-driven automation. Our approach targets context-free diagram families represented via context-free gramm, with equational constraints between such families modeled using grammar-level rewrite rules. Our framework unifies the representation of both concrete string diagram reasoning and context-free family reasoning through double-pushout (dpo) graph rewriting and context-free gramm, respectively. We aim to demonstrate that our model captures the essence of string diagram reasoning meaningfully and assess the system for practical implementation. Additionally, the validity will have to verify soundness to the existing abstract semantics of string diagram rewriting and assess the usability in software by verifying certain computability properties essential to automated systems based around a wide-set representation.

Estimating the precision matrix (the inverse covariance matrix) is primarily used to identify conditional dependencies among continuous variables. However, the impact of outliers becomes amplified in high-dimensional scenarios as the dimensionality grows. To address this, we introduce a robust estimation method for the inverse covariance matrix utilizing an $l_1$-regularized framework with a weighted sample covariance. The robustness of our approach is validated using a nonparametric method based on the integrated squared error criterion. To mitigate the objective function's non-concivity, we formulate a majorization-based minimization-like algorithm for efficient optimization. Furthermore, we establish the estimator's asymptotic consistency. We evaluate the proposed method against several existing approaches through numerical simulations, and finally, we illustrate its effectiveness using applications in genetic network inference.

This research tackles actuator selection for active flow control by introducing a new reinforcement learning framework. The method leverages an initially pre-trained agent designed for numerous actuators; it predicts how the removal of potential actuators affects value function metrics, thereby indicating performance shifts tested across two scenarios: the 1-dimensional Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation and laminar two-dimensional flow over an airfoil at Re=1000 (angles of attack between 12–20 degrees), effectively demonstrating its strengths and constraints. The introduced actuator sparsification strategy operates on sequential removal starting with a complete configuration by ranking components based on their influence on these metrics. Although constrained by the inherent limitation of sequential removal, the generated patterns demonstrate significant performance capabilities, enabling precise approximations of the Pareto front representing actuator expenses.

This paper introduces an novel approach to addressing the problem of semantic enrichment within mathematical expression. The solution integrates statistical machine translation with disambiguation techniques that leverage text surrounding these expressions. Process begins with a Support Vector Machine classifier that resolves the ambiguity of mathematical terms by analyzing both visual presentation forms and adjacent context. Subsequently, those disambiguation results are utilized to refine the semantic enrichment of a statistical machine translation-based system. In our experiments, demonstrated improvements surpass prior systems' capabilities.

Gravitational wave memory refers to a permanent imprint of space distorted by signals from merging binary black hole systems. These memory events collectively form a stochastic background, the Stochastic Gravitational Wave Memory Background (SGWMB). Our analysis reveals that SGWMB exhibits Brownian motion, meaning its Power Spectral Density (PSD) scales as $1/f^2$, where $f$ is frequency, and the signal's magnitude is dictated by the rate of black hole mergers. Unlike conventional non-memory stochastic backgrounds from binary mergers, which are limited by high-frequency cutoff points at merger frequencies, the Brownian nature of the memory component extends into significantly higher frequencies as well. This extended range implies that SGWMB dominates in the higher-frequency spectrum, and failure to isolate it properly would lead it to be mistaken as standard non-memory background noise. Correctly investigating this component could enable LIGO to identify populations of supermassive binary black hole systems. Furthermore, the analysis of the SGWMB not only introduces novel methods for detecting gravitational wave memory itself but also offers a new observational avenue for probing gravitational theory.

Determining optimal variables for adjusting confounds remains a pivotal challenge in assessing exposure effects within observational research, attracting significant attention recently in the field of causal inference. However, standard routine approaches suffer from major drawbacks, specifically that no finite sample size ensures they will produce exposure effect estimators and confidence intervals meeting performance standards with certainty. This project addresses the difficulty of inferring conditional causal hazard ratios from non-experimental data under the assumption of no unmeasured confounding. The critical obstacle specific to survival analysis is the existence of key confounding variables distinct from those defining the censoring mechanism; this issue is resolved in the current paper by introducing a straightforward novel procedure implementable via off-the-shelf penalized Cox regression software. Specifically, we introduce hypothesis tests to determine if an exposure impacts a designated survival endpoint that are consistent with theoretical requirements even without assuming any specific covariates possess effects (under standard conditions that only a few coefficients are zero). Furthermore, simulation analyses demonstrate the efficacy of these new techniques for generating reliable conclusions, particularly in the presence of high-dimensional covariates.

We return our attention to the spatial ${\lambda}$-Fleming-Viot originally outlined in [1], focusing specifically on $T_0$, the epoch reaching back to the common ancestor of two lineages. This inquiry splits according to whether the dynamics unfold across the complete two-dimensional plane or are constrained to a finite rectangle. By employing a differential equation that relates the common ancestor time to the spatial or physical separation of the respective trajectories, we derive simplified approximation methods of considerable accuracy for both configurations. Ultimately, this analytical framework also allows us to investigate whether the genealogical evolution inherent to this model transitions out to infinity in finite time, providing further illumination on a problem partially explored in [2].

The article investigates a Cauchy problem for Helmholtz equations, famously characterized by solutions sensitive enough to become exponentially unstable when input errors fluctuate. Within the framework of the quasi-reversibility method, Fourier truncation is employed to deliberately perturb the original problem. By transforming this modified problem into an associated hyperbolic equation, which represents a key component of the approach, a stable approximate solution can achieve. Furthermore, specific bounds are derived regarding errors between theoretical exact solutions and numerical approximations as a function of noise intensity; this analysis also demonstrates stability in a Lipschitz manner concerning noise variations and validates the effectiveness of the numerical algorithm via illustrative example.

Recent years have witnessed substantial advancements in few-shot learning, a paradigm particularly effective at addressing the heavy class imbalance encountered in anomaly detection, a challenging problem realm. We introduce an innovative few-shot classification method that leverages a database of several pre-trained convolutional models as the backbone of our architecture. By incorporating a unique ensembling strategy, our framework enhances overall accuracy while significantly reducing the number of parameters, which fosters feasibility for real-time applications. Following an exhaustive hyperparameter search powered by a power-line defect detection dataset, our model achieved a 92.30% accuracy on the 5-way/5-shot task. Consequently, when evaluated against existing state-of-the-art methods without additional tuning, our model surpassed their performance on competitive standards.

Hard disk systems are frequently regarded as models for simple liquids. Within statistical mechanics, the hard disk configuration space is typically divided by acting on various symmetry groups. Research examines how these quotienting processes alter both the topological and geometrical characteristics of the configuration space for few-disk systems on square and hexagonal tori. A specific metric is established on both the configuration space and its various quotient counterparts that maintains the intended symmetries. This metric facilitates the construction of precise triangulations of these spaces, represented as $\alpha$-complexes. Critical point regions in configuration space correspond to topological alterations resulting from variations in disk radius; it is theorized these points correlate with the configurational entropy observed in glassy phases and may explain phase transition origins in diverse systems. The count and intrinsic topological and geometrical attributes of these critical points were found to shift based on the specific symmetries employed when reducing the configuration space through quotienting.

Furthermore, we investigate factors such as averaging duration, spatial refinement settings (and the effect of higher-order methods), and time steps. The code's performance, tested in different mesh and time step conditions and with varying values for energy dissipation, is compared with other studies. For a standard solution code (and not for an "improved" variant like ILCES), the grid resolution impacts efficiency and computational cost is low. We also perform sensitivity analyses with time step size on various factors and discuss how the code's parameters relate to available data from prior studies. Finally, this work shows that our understanding can also improve other types of work by revealing that the code's efficiency is highly sensitive to grid resolution, spatial refinement settings (like "Lethal"), and time steps.

In decision-making scenarios involving a balance between exploration and exploitation, conservatism is a valuable trait. To address this, we introduce \emph{$C^4$-bandit}, a new cascading contextual online game that integrates this conservative mechanism. To tackle this challenge, we develop the $C^4$-UCB algorithm and establish $n$-step upper regret bounds for cases with both known and unknown baseline rewards. The derived regret decompose into two components: (1) the bound associated with general contextual combinatorial cascading bandits, and (2) a constant accounting for the penalty imposed by the conservative mechanism. We introduce a novel framework for measuring homophily in networks with categorical nodes, specifically those divided into discrete classes such as different colors. Our analysis applies this method to two network categories: (i) protein-protein interaction networks where node classes reflect functional roles and edges indicate functional associations, and (ii) Pokec online networks where node segmentation is based on user age and edges denote friendship. Consistent with established methods, the approach evaluates the relative density of edges within each induced class substructure against what density would be anticipated under a null model. Our unique contribution lies in constructing an endogenous null model where the sample space is derived from the input data, enabling the precise analytical derivation of z-scores and related statistics for relative class density. These Tchebycheff-corrected z-scores provide a direct quantification of the statistical significance of observed homophily. Each z-score's calculation incorporates specific network structures through combinatorial invariants, notably the counts of subgraphs featuring two spanning edges. Furthermore, individual z-scores can be calculated in O(n + m) time for networks with n nodes and m edges, ensuring an overall computational approach for assessing homophily that remains efficiently streamlined and results in the analysis of homophily and related isolation statistics. To avoid isolated nodes, the analysis counts isolated nodes of each induced class, calculated in O(nm). Theoretical findings demonstrate that, consistent with preliminary observations, both protein networks and online networks exhibit significant levels of homophily regarding the defined node characteristics.

With advancements in quantum computing hardware, potential applications are increasingly pursued; yet, practical implementations continue to be limited by device noise, specifically affecting low-fidelity two-qubit gates. Grasping how electronic excitations move within conjugated polymers is pivotal for developing advanced optoelectronic technologies, including solar cells, OLEDs, and flexible devices. Although crystalline variants can be analyzed using solid-state methods leveraging lattice periodicity, amorphous polymers pose challenges due to their intermediate disorder state and lack of symmetry. Applying this framework allows for an investigation into exciton transport across different morphologies and temperatures. Exciton behavior includes a thermalization phase whose characteristics hinge on the balance between thermal energy, electronic coupling strengths, and varying degrees of disorder, leading to distinct transport regimes. By modeling representative poly(p-phenylene vinylene) (PPV) systems, our study illuminates the impacts of temperature and disorder on localisation, charge separation, non-equilibrium dynamics, and the attainability of thermal equilibrium for excitons in amorphous polymers.

The rapid growth of trigger-action mechanisms in Internet-of-Things (IoT) environments has made vulnerabilities stemming from inter-device interactions increasingly common. Experimental evaluations using PEEVES datasets demonstrate the system's high proficiency in reconstructing accurate event sequences from sensor readings and pinpointing pivotal attack targets with minimal human intervention.

The largest stars are believed to eject a considerable portion of their mass through steady winds while on the main sequence as blue supergiants, shaping their subsequent evolution, core-collapse supernovae, and impact on the ionization of the interstellar medium along with the enrichment of chemical elements. While past research has relied heavily on collisional "density-squared" indicators—specifically free-free radio emission and optical lines like Hα, which have seen recent attention—these tools demand substantial correction in environments with extensive wind clumping. Overcoming this complexity and refining "density-squared" mass-loss measurements necessitate high-resolution, high-fidelity time-resolved spectroscopy of UV resonances. We employed a collection of idealised N-body simulations to evaluate the consequences of artificial heating of star particles by dark matter particles on the kinematics and structural properties of simulated galactic discs. Our analysis reveals that this nonphysical collisional heating causes an overall rise in the stellar velocity dispersion ($\sigma_\phi$), while their average rotational velocities ($\overline{v}_\phi$) correspondingly drop. The heating rate is governed mainly by the quantity of dark matter halo particles—or, for a constant halo mass, the individual dark matter particle mass—along with radial gradients in the localized dark matter density within the disc; it shows little dependence on stellar particle mass. Galaxies housed in haloes resolved with fewer than roughly $10^6$ dark matter particles are exceptionally vulnerable to artificial morphological distortions, a sensitivity independent of the total halo mass (requiring an even larger resolution for the galactic center region). This collisional heating causes otherwise flattened galactic discs to become rounder and spheroid-like, leading to the loss of rotational support. Furthermore, it shifts galaxies into incorrect positions on common observational scaling relations; at fixed stellar mass, the effect inflates galaxy sizes while lowering mean specific angular momentum and rotational speeds. We therefore advise careful interpretation of mass-scaled simulated galaxy relationships when applied to low-mass regimes where these artificial collisional biases may skew normalization, slopes, and scatter.

In partially observable reinforcement learning settings, offline learning enables the utilization of hidden information, such as the underlying system state, which is typically inaccessible during online deployment. This work analyzes asymmetric actor-critic frameworks employing state-based critics, identifying core flaws that compromise a prevalent variant and constrain its efficacy in handling partial observability. Our analysis dissects the problem by separating each communication channel system into two distinct groups: diffusers and boundary; we then introduce the relationship between transmission frequency thresholds, distance communication ranges by the use of a frequency-transfer function through a set of equations. Few-shot graph classification endeavors to determine labels for new graphs based on a small set of available training examples per category. Existing approaches attempt to overcome the scarcity of labels by integrating few-shot learning mechanisms, enabling rapid adaptation to target tasks. Typically, this involves aggregating knowledge across diverse meta-training settings and generalizing that understanding to a disjoint set in the final test. Unfortunately, most current methodologies assume meta-training tasks are independent, thereby neglecting beneficial correlations between them, which, if exploited effectively, could significantly improve model generalization. Yet, incorporating these task relationships remains difficult due to the intricate nature of a high volume of training tasks. Our solutions involve a novel framework called FAITH, which models these dependencies using a hierarchical task structure built at various scales, coupled with a loss-driven sampling technique to prioritize highly correlated task clusters. Additionally, a specialized classifier per meta-task leverages these learned associations to enhance few-shot performance. Comprehensive tests on standard benchmark datasets illustrate FAITH's substantial gains compared to current state-of-the-art approaches.

The dominant bottleneck in contemporary Von-Neumann architectures handling processing-to-storage data transfer, particularly during Artificial Intelligence applications, has been effectively addressed by computing-on-memory (CiM) solutions that promise lower power usage and latency. While traditional analog CiM methods face significant reliability challenges compromising accuracy, recent digitized input and weight approaches have improved trustiness but remain inefficient in their use of inherent digital characteristics to lower power draws. Consequently, we propose a new technique to enhance power efficiency by employing a Modified Radix-4 Booth algorithm for the input data stream and Modified Canonical Signed Digit encoding for the load network weights. Results indicate that integrating M-RD4 and M-CSD reduces the ratio of 1×1 hardware units for LeNet and AlexNet models by 78.1% and 80.13%, yielding an average of 84% improvement in hardware usage efficiency. Furthermore, the proposed method reaches 94% computing efficiency compared with previous works, with a peak fixed-point throughput of 9.013 TOPS on 98.1383s/s energy.

Finally, we present experimental results, highlighting how this methodology offers clear advantages in scenarios where supervised learning proves infeasible.

To solve this, the paper introduces training on fewer, more strategic annotation points, specifically by analyzing video footage instead of just still frames. When gathered sequentially from videos, existing DensePose labels can be significantly amplified and propagated across frames leveraging natural motion cues as a "free boost." The study presents "DensePose-Track," a video dataset where only intermittent frames receive traditional DensePose labeling. Extensive experimentation shows that these combined annotation improvements substantially outperform robust baselines. Additionally, despite previous suggestions that synthetically creating generic motions via geometric warps of single images might suffice, this research demonstrates that such techniques yield poor compared to performance and validates that motion cues derived authentically from video sequences are significantly superior.

During intrauterine growth, the fetal cortical plate (CP) experiences significant structural alterations; thus, monitoring its development and folding is crucial for evaluating fetal brain maturation. Our approach is two-pronged: first, we adapt a multi-dimensional topology-based loss function to improve topological precision; second, we introduce a novel "hole ratio" metric to quantify topological defects relative to the structure's scale. We validated this method on two public datasets comprising 27 fetal brain MRI scans using complementary overlap, distance, and topology-based evaluation measures. This study investigates correlation clustering through a fairness-lens perspective. In standard correlation clustering, we are provided a complete graph with positive and negatively-labeled edges; the objective involves identifying a vertex partition that minimizes disagreement metrics. These include counting the number of intra-cluster negatively-labeled edges as well as the number of inter-cluster positively-labeled edges.

We examine two variations of fair correlation constraints where vertices are colored and clusters are formed to avoid the overrepresentation of any single color class. The first variant seeks clusterings that equalize the feature (such as gender) distribution within clusters to match the global distribution. In specific instances where clusters must maintain a $1:p$ ratio between node features, we developed an $\mathcal O(p^2)$-approximation algorithm, which is further demonstrated with a generalization to colors beyond just two. Additionally, we prove that solving this specific problem strictly under equality constraints is NP-hard. The second version applies relative lower and upper bounds regarding each color's count per cluster. Our goal is to optimize clustering performance by adhering strictly to these capacity constraints while simultaneously minimizing the number of disagreements. Finally, beyond our theoretical contributions, we reinforce the algorithmic efficacy through an empirical study on real world data.

Currently, heart rate (HR) tracking utilizing photoplethysmography (PPG), a cornerstone feature in almost all wrist-worn gadgets, becomes compromised by limb movements. While this limitation is often mitigated through data fusion with inertial measurement units—and deep learning algorithms for this purpose have emerged—they remain too sophisticated for mobile devices in consumer attire and lack result transparency. In this piece, we unveil "PULSE," a bespoke deep learning architecture leveraging temporal convolution and comprehensive cross-at-tention heads that not only enhance sensor fusion efficiency but also advance outcome interpretability. Extensive validation over three open repositories showcases an error reduction of 7.56 % mean absolute error on PPG-DaLiA compared to existing models, which is likely to establish records of this scale. This paper presents an approach to retrieve specific domain concepts from vast Linked Open Data (LOD) reservoirs, aiming to support the development of targeted ontologies enriched with field-aware knowledge and definitions. The core strategy involves defining "search entities" by connecting LOD vocabularies with technical terminology specific to the target domain. Leveraging these entities serves as the launchpad to access higher-level ontology classes, during which common class occurrences and hierarchical pathways are analyzed to reveal meaningful conceptual connections. Furthermore, technical index registers alongside natural language processing techniques employ a filtering assessment to validate that extracted concepts comprehensively address the target domain. For illustration, the method was successfully applied to construct a class hierarchy and ontology focusing on polymers and their physical properties using Wikidata as the primary dataset source. Beyond its demonstrated success, the methodology can handle any general dataset with structured class hierarchies and aims to equip ontology developers with the tools to build preliminary conceptual models tailored to their specific projects.

Inspired by the side-by-side swimming and mid-dispatch synchronization behaviors of red-nose tetra fish, this study utilized numerical simulations to analyze how abrupt shifts in phase angles affect unsteady wake dynamics around pitch-side-by-side foils. Operating at a Reynolds number of $Re = 4,000$ and a Strouhal number of $St = 0.5$, the analysis focused on four distinct hybrid swimming modes; two involved an immediate $π$ phase shift during the 20th oscillation cycle, while the other two mimicked burst-and-coast locomotion by suspending oscillation briefly (two cycles) before applying a similar phase change. In every scenario, the foils transitioned from initial out-of-phase pitching to in-phase motion, either initiating an upstroke or a downstroke, which triggered a split wake configuration characterized by a growing secondary vortex street situated between two primary streets. Importantly, while the growth rate of this secondary street remained constant across all four modes, the phase-switching maneuver nearly equalized pressure distributions above and below both foils, thereby significantly reducing side force.

Robots have greatly benefitted from deep learning, particularly through deep reinforcement learning, which has proven highly effective at creating neural network controllers for numerous applications. Despite this practical success, relying solely on these algorithms without theoretical backing creates a significant limitation: the absence of rigorous performance guarantees, specifically regarding stability metrics like the Lyapunov condition. This stands in sharp contrast to traditional, model-based control methods (e.g., LQR) that can design controllers with mathematically proven stability capabilities. To bridge this divide, we present a versatile framework that synthesizes neural network controllers satisfying Lyapunov stability constraints alongside dedicated neural network Lyapunov functions for verification. We frame the process of verifying the Lyapunov condition within mixed-integer linear programming (MIP). Depending on whether the MIP succeeds or fails in verifying the original policy's convergence to the primary goal, our verifier provides corresponding counter examples designed to improve the controller and function candidates alongside stability confirmation. We implement code designed with computing the region of attraction as well. We use this on robots such as inverted pendulums and quadrotors while showing that the neural network controller produces superior performance than baseline linear controllers, with our code available on GitHub.

Generative Adversarial Networks, and specifically StyleGAN, have emerged as dominant methods in image synthesis. StyleGAN, celebrated for its exceptional visual fidelity and adaptability in numerous downstream tasks, serves as a key area of study in recent literature. This report details the StyleGAN architecture, examines its applications since introduction, and critically evaluates its constraints. It is designed to assist both newcomers entering the field and experienced researchers seeking updates on current methodologies and toolchains. Central to its appeal are the learned properties of the latent space, which remains well-structured and disentangled despite being trained without supervision; this combination of structural integrity and high-quality image generation facilitates editing capabilities unmatched by previous methods with only another such model. However, the influence exerted by users is restricted to images generated within StyleGAN's learned distribution, highlighting the necessity of GAN inversion and latent style transformation techniques to apply such control to authentic images. Research into these inversion methods has illuminated the generator's internal mechanics and inherent boundaries. By analyzing these dynamics and established visual priors utilized for discriminatory tasks, we explore the reasons behind StyleGAN's status as the preferred generator. Forward-looking insights identify current gaps, suggest potential refinements through fine-tuned generation for particular tasks, and forecast evolving research trajectories that may overcome these limitations while deepening our capacity to manipulate and leverage GAN-embedded representations.

End-to-end automatic speech recognition (ASR) targets a universal representation of speech, yet there is a scarcity of analytical tools designed to decipher internal mechanisms or the impact of hierarchical relationships in model architectures. Understanding layer-to-layer representation correlations is vital for uncovering the link between neural dynamics and performance. Although techniques like correlation analysis have been applied elsewhere in the field, such studies have previously been neglected in End-to-End ASR investigations. This research employs Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA), a technique adapted from Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCCA), to investigate internal inter-layer dynamics within CNN-based Convolutional Neural Network, LSTM-based Recurrent, and Transformer-based systems. Findings reveal that neural layers in Convolutional models exhibit increasing hierarchical dependency as depth deepens, a phenomenon primarily visible when representations share closer correlations; however, LSTM structures do not demonstrate such a pattern despite showing a gradual bottom-up progression throughout training. In contrast, Transformer encoder layers present inconsistent efficiency-related correlations with increased model depth. Collectively, these findings elucidate the varying role architectural design plays in shaping speech recognition outcomes, offering these specific methods as diagnostic tools to guide the development of superior models, particularly within Convolutional architectures. The results indicate that neural systems behave largely like multi-scale deep convolution operators (MSSN), with clearer hierarchical dependency observable in Convolutional models and a notable correlation between intermediate and deeper Transformer layers during training.

Although recent breakthroughs have emerged regarding communication learning, most existing efforts have concentrated on mimicking human language protocols. Biological cooperation naturally generates a diverse array of signaling structures with varying complexities. In light of this, we investigate the broader landscape of natural communication by focusing on low-level, emergent implicit signaling within decentralized, multi-agent learning contexts characterized by sparse and difficult reward signals. To address the challenges of coordinating under such scarce rewards, we introduce a curriculum-driven framework comprising: (1) velocity-shaped environmental design customized to the team's current capability level, and (2) a behavioral curriculum that ensures masters of single-agent strategies succeed as a foundational step before tackling multi-agent dynamics. Experimental results on pursuit-evasion scenarios demonstrate that this strategy induces superior coordination compared to sophisticated analytical and learned alternatives. Notably, our method achieves success when pursuers possess only 50% the speed of evaders, outmatching top-performing baselines which fail when limited to 80% speed. Furthermore, analyzing position-dependent social influence reveals significant reliance on information exchange; pursuers trained via our approach utilize more than double the information transfer (measured in bits) of baseline methods, confirming the robust learning of implicit signaling mechanisms.

Driven by rapid population increases and urban expansion, severe traffic congestion has become a persistent challenge for major metropolitan areas. While various historical strategies—from widening roads to managing transportation demand—have been attempted, specifically including congestion pricing as a punitive measure, this project focuses on a distinct positive-reinforcement approach. We propose an algorithm that enhances network efficiency and alleviates congestion by providing drivers with personalized incentives to alternate their paths. Leaping smart devices, we created an mechanism that delivers these rewards based on individual driver preferences and real-time, aggregated traffic data. These incentives follow solutions to large-scale optimizations designed either to minimize total travel time or other network costs, such as carbon emissions. Addressing the need for continuous solving of these enormous optimization tasks within the network, we devised a distributed computational framework. This proposed algorithm proves guaranteed convergence under minimal assumptions and is validated with empirical data. Testing the system with Los Angeles-area traffic records yielded an average of 11% reduction in congestion on both major arterials and highways.

We present "Bayesian Bits," an efficient strategy combining mixed-precision quantization and pruning using the gradient optimization framework. By decomposing the quantization process to sequentially evaluate a doubled bit width, the approach handles the difference between a full precision input and the previously rounded value by quantizing the resulting residual. The method then determines whether to revert to this quantized residual as part of the output layer to achieve a larger data size or reduce error. Starting from an initial bit width of a power of two ensures the final output aligns with hardware capabilities. Moreover, the approach supports pruning by adding an extra option to use the zero-bit level, providing a holistic framework that addresses precision and pruning simultaneously. Through this method, the authors incorporate learnable, gate mechanisms across layers. By optimizing approximate values over this model setup—while assuming a prior belief where these elements should generally switch off—it is possible to simulate lower-bit operations using only a subset of the original components as zeros. By testing various scenarios on different test datasets to assess our approach on available datasets, the authors have shown significant improvement over fixed precision and mixed-precision levels for achieving more reliable results.

Although often obscure, the famous Machian principle proposes a purely relational foundation for physical theory, completely excluding "absolute space." In classical mechanics, extending standard symmetries along these lines yields equations of motion where the particle experiences effective inertial fields, which originate from the total mass distribution of the system rather than a fixed background. This paper adopts the same strategy, recasting non-relativistic quantum mechanics—specifically the Schrödinger equation—with full Machean underpinnings. The quantized analog mirrors the classical approach by being strictly relational regarding the particles' positions and momenta within a physical configuration, effectively eradicating any concept of Absolute space.

Addressing this challenge introduces Mixture of Experts Generative Adversarial Networks (MEGAN), an ensemble framework comprising several specialized generator networks. Unlike prior methods that require manual clustering steps to organize different modalities, MEGAN employs an end-to-end training strategy where gating networks automatically select the relevant generator based on specific conditions. This selection is facilitated by a reparameterization technique that ensures continuous gradient flow despite the categorical nature of generator choice during decision-making. Results show that distinct generators successfully learn unique and critical data segments, delivering a MS-SSIM score of 0.247 on the CelebA dataset and an inception score of 8.33 on a non-supervised basis to CIFAR-10.

The Taylor expansion-based, cosmologic approach, applied to the Hubble function, serves as a technique for studying cosmic evolution via cosmological data. Consequently, this study utilizes the SNIa (Pantheon sample) and Hubble datasets to critically evaluate the strengths and limitations of the cosmologic method. Additionally, two other established model-independent methods—Gaussian processes and genetic algorithms—are employed alongside it to determine functional dynamics. For comparison, the results were benchmarked against the concordance $\Lambda$CDE model under the assumption that it holds validity. However, our findings indicate that cosmologic method results lack the necessary precision when compared to alternative approaches. Specifically, based on the less constrained Hubble data, the parameter estimates for $q_0$ and $j_0$ yield results that deviate from the most robust $\lambda$CDE outcome by over $3\sigma$ tension. Ultimately, whether applying either or both datasets, our analysis concludes that cosmographie proves inferior due to inherent biases, rendering it unsuitable for accurate function reconstruction at greater redshifts compared to its alternatives.

Using the path integral Monte Carlo (PIMC) method to analyze thermal densities, this study examines the thermal characteristics of a two-dimensional dipolar gas where dipole polarization is not perpendicular to the plane. As confirmed, two-dimensional systems exhibit the standard Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) behavior during superfluid-to-normal transitions; our simulations reveal that both the resulting anisotropic gas and stripe phases adhere to these BKT scaling laws. Specifically, increasing the tilting angle at a fixed density lowers the critical temperature as the system shifts from a gas to a striped state. Superfluidity transverse to the stripes exhibits low magnitude near the critical point, though it grows significantly as temperatures drop, occurring primarily during the approach to the gas-neighbor transition. These qualitative findings resonate with reported observations of supersolidity recently seen in a near-one-dimensional series of dipolar drops where a perpendicular dimension may be involved.

Binary code author analysis is crucial across various software engineering contexts. This research formalizes the binary authorship verification process to mirror the real-world workflows of forensic investigators. Specifically, it seeks to identify if an unidentified binary was created by a particular developer, even given only limited sample codes and where the actual programmer might fall outside the known set of candidates. We introduce an efficient framework, BinMLM. Trained on opcode sequence traces derived from control flow graphs, it defines programming behaviors unique to potential authors. Furthermore, BinMLM employs an architecture mixing shared representations with specific encoding gate structures to learn how candidates combine general programming traits, thereby addressing issues related to scarce training data. Its optimization process combines external pre-training, joint training, and fine-tuning to neutralize extraneous noise and isolate distinctive stylistic markers. Comprehensive testing on Codeforces and the Google Code Jam datasets yields strong performance, with improvements over state-of-the-art baselines reaching up to 19.46%, demonstrating resilience in multi-author environments. Additionally, BinMLM effectively assesses organizations by analyzing a real-world Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) dataset, offering critical clues about groups behind cyber attacks.

Effectively communicating novel research concepts requires emphasizing their relationship and distinctions with previous literature. Our approach employs two stages: a content planning phase that produces a tree of relevant citations and a subsequent surface realization phase that transforms this structural skeleton into fluent prose. On a new dataset hosted on the ACL Antholini based around these work-related sections, our model surpasses several leading existing summarizers and multi-document models.

Consequently, we facilitate continuous evaluation of the discrete output by constructing the output from simulating a functional framework.

This study presents the crystal structure, thermodynamic attributes, and the performance achieved via adiabatic demagnetization refrigeration (ADR) in the spin-7/2 triangular antiferromagnet KBaGd(BO3)2. The material undergoes magnetic ordering at $T_N = 263$ mK in zero field, following an exchange between nearest-neighbor spins averaging 44 mK. Test runs using the PPMS equipment succeeded in reaching a minimum temperature of $T_{min} = 122$ mK—nearly double $T_N$—while delivering a hold time exceeding 8 hours and an entropy storage capacity of 192 $^/$mK$\,$cm$^3$. Both metrics represent substantial progress surpasses the spin-1/2 Yb$^{3+}$ analogue. We propose that the superior cooling arises because KBaGd(BO3)2 features a balanced competition between dipolar and exchange interactions; when combined with geometric frustration and structural disorder, these factors drive the final cold temperature significantly below $T_N$, enhancing cooling efficacy.

Normalizing flows offer a sophisticated way to compute tractable probability density estimates from known distributions through the application of invertible transformations. However, the primary difficulty lies in enhancing model expressiveness without violating strict invertibility requirements. To overcome this, we propose embedding localized self-attention mechanisms. Since traditional attention operations do not inherently satisfy invertibility, they cannot be trivially integrated into standard normalizing flows; therefore, to enable this integration, we suggest using contractive flows instead. Building on this, we present Attentive Contractive Flow (ACF), leveraging these specialized flow-based generative models. Crucially, ACF allows for the seamless, plug-in augmentation of state-of-the-art flow architectures. Experimental evidence demonstrates that this integration enhances representational capabilities—evident in lower bits-per-dimension metrics—as well as accelerating training convergence. Further qualitative analysis, featuring image interpolations, confirms a marked improvement in the visual quality of generated samples and a precise capture of data-dependent local structures. Additionally, perturbations via Additive White Gaussian Noise testing indicate a greater and more reliable robustness in ACF variants compared to the dot-product attention baseline.

PYROBOCOP serves as an accessible, lightweight Python toolkit designed for controlling and optimizing robots whose dynamics are defined by nonlinear Differential Algebraic Equations (DAEs), with a specific capability to address contact problems modeled through complementarity conditions. This process generates mathematical tasks that belong to the class known as Mathematical Programs with Complementarity Constraints (MPCOs), which are notoriously difficult for standard NonLinear Program (NLP) solvers because they typically do not uphold standard constraint qualifications and demand specialized techniques for effective handling. PYROBOCOP automates the restructuring of these constraints, allowing existing NLP solvers to efficiently manage robotic optimization problems. Additionally, its strengths are underscored by comparative performance analyses relative to other open-source alternatives, such as CasAdi and Pyomo, in the field of nonlinear optimization for dynamic systems.

Spatial perception challenges serve as foundational elements for robot kinematics and computer vision, yet real-world scenarios frequently contaminate observations with outliers that degrade traditional estimation solvers. By adapting the established Otsu's algorithm from image processing for statistical threshold selection—which optimizes separation via between-class variance—the method ensures optimal clustering. Additionally, a multi-layered application of this thresholding process is designed within the iterative structure to reliably distinguish inliers that may be overshadowed even amid a majority of outliers. Experimental evaluations across rotation averaging, pose search, sensor data alignment, category-based registration, and SLAM demonstrate the estimator's efficacy in filtering up to 70% to 90% outlier corruption typically. The IMOT method consistently converges within 3 to 10 iterations. It achieves convergence rates 3 to 125 times faster than existing approaches such as GNC or the adaptive estimator, without requiring prior knowledge of the noise bounds.

Addressing the group synchronization problem requires estimating a comprehensive collection of group values from noisy pairwise data measurements. Found in critical computations, particularly within single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) for 3D molecular reconstruction, standard estimators typically use iterative linear and nonlinear operations that do not guarantee optimal results. Leveraging structural analogies to deep neural networks through algorithm unrolling, training data is utilized to optimize the procedures. We have constructed such unrolled algorithms for various synchronisation scenarios alongside multi-reference alignment. Numerical evaluations demonstrate across diverse situations that this strategy surpasses current synchronization methods.

The influence of electromagnetic interactions from colliding beam bunches on the Tevatron's beam dynamics offered diverse insights, enabling significant advancements in simulation models and analytical tools. This research analyzes the bright main-sequence eclipsing binary WOCS 11028 (Sanders 617) located within the M67 open cluster, which exhibits a single eclipse per orbit despite missing typical second-light events, yet allows for the determination of stellar masses in great precision ($M_A = 1.222 \pm 0.006\ M_\odot$; $M_B = 0.909 \pm 0.004\ M_\odot$) through a rigorous constraint on inclination. Rather than utilizing precise radii obtainable from double eclipses, this work applies a spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting technique instead, achieving detailed SED deconvolution that identifies the primary star ($WOCS 11028\ A$) at the faint main-sequence turnoff in M67—an evolutionary stage postdating convective core creation but preceding the main-sequence hook, while the star cools. These observational results contradict evolutionary models assuming solar metallicity; matching the object's characteristics requires metal enrichment above that level of SOlar status. Consequently, to align spectroscopic M67 abundances with models, the introduction of diffusion processes and a reduction in the magnitude of convective overshoot for these turnoff stars is suggested. Ultimately, under super-solar bulk metallicity assumptions, multiple diagnostics place the M67 cluster age between 3.5 and 4.0 billion years.

Type-C quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs), prevalent in the low-frequency range during the hard spectral state of X-ray binaries, are best explained by the Lenz-Thirring precession of an inner hot, geometrically thick accretion flow misoriented relative to the black hole spin axis. Previous studies, however, neglected the gravitational influence of the surrounding truncated thin-disc often present in this configuration. To address this gap, we conducted general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) simulations of misaligned systems featuring these truncated disc structures. Our findings confirm that while the inner flow remains prone to precession, the rate is drastically reduced—amounting to only 5% of that theoretical for an isolated torus. This retardation results from angular momentum transfer interactions between the outer thin-disc and the inner thick flow. The implications of this mechanism for understanding Type-C QPOs have subsequently been discussed.

Digital privacy has become a critical element of information and communications technology (ICT) infrastructure. Although various techniques for digital privacy protection exist, such as cryptography, network security, and access control, the levels of accessible safeguards still do not meet all needs, highlighting a disparity we refer to as the Digital Privacy Divide (DPD). This research investigates this gap within ICT ecosystems. First, we conduct an online survey via crowdsourcing, gathering input from 776 participants to better understand the scale and nature of the DPD phenomenon. Second, we develop a factor-analysis-driven statistical approach to generate a DPD index, reducing survey data into a single metric; this index measures the privacy divide across eight specific survey questions. Third, we apply a DPD proportional odds model to examine how socio-demographic characteristics correlate with a user's relative risk in the digital economy. Rigorous validation, such as a Cronbach's $\alpha$ score of $0.92$, confirms the survey's internal reliability, and the analysis demonstrates that the calculated index effectively encapsulates the underlying correlations among privacy variables. Ultimately, the proportional odds model reveals significant statistical links between user status in the privacy divide and age, specifically indicating that individuals under the age of 33 tend to be more privacy-conscious than those aged 33 and older.

Transfer Entropy (TE), serving as a generalization of Granger Causality, evaluates "information transfer" between a source and a target signal by disregarding the target's inherent self-predictability when quantifying interrelationships. Narrowband signals, often believed to represent intrinsic brain activities and typically isolated using band-pass filters in neuroscience, serve as prime examples in this context, yet the application of classic TE to narrow-band signals is generally discouraged. Our simulations on simplistic examples substantiate this limitation, revealing that traditional TE implementations struggle to correctly recover interaction delays and effect sizes when applied to narrow-band inputs. We introduce a novel approach wherein the inputs are whitened before calculating a bivariate measure of directional, time-lagged dependencies; this modification successfully resolves the deficiencies identified in conventional systems with such input types, as shown in these simulation scenarios. Subsequently, we examined the performance of this measure on delta and theta response segments from Magnetoencephalography (MEG) data recorded in reaction to continuous speech. Our analysis indicated that weak effects observed in directed interactions from stimulus to neural responses are pronounced in the theta band relative to the delta band, implying that the latter reflects predictive coupling more strongly, whereas the former underpins reactive processing from sensory inputs to brain areas. Ultimately, we aim to bolster scholarly engagement toward employing directional measures to uncover these specific frequency-based dependencies.

This study examines diffusive four-terminal magnetic Josephson junctions in cross-shaped lead arrangements within the weak proximity limit. Using the linearized Keldysh-Usadel approach, we derive analytical expressions for the anomalous Green's function and Josephson current via the quasiclassical theory combined with the Fourier series method; these results naturally revert to those of non-magnetic junctions when the exchange field vanishes. Our findings indicate that increasing the thickness of the magnetic barrier can invert the supercurrent direction entering certain leads, though currents at other leads maintain their flow. The direction of this reversion can be toggled by adjusting perpendicular superconducting phases. Even without magnetic fields, we demonstrate that supercurrent flow can be modulated by altering phase differences perpendicularly. Consequently, we propose a viable pathway for developing nanoscale superconducting phase transistors built around our proposed junction, leveraging its rich phase-switching properties as a functional core.

Nanometer-thick rare-earth-transition metal (RE-TM) alloys, characterized by their precisely engineered compositions and robust out-of-plane magnetic anisotropy, are currently the subject of intense research for applications involving ultrafast magnetophotonics. However, simultaneously achieving the lateral nanosizing essential for device miniaturization and retaining tunable optomagnetic performance along with preserved magnetic anisotropy remains a significant challenge. In this work, we embed nanoscale Tb$_{18}$Co$_{82}$ ferrimagnetic particles—including strong out-of-plane magnetic anisotropy—with gold plasmonic nanoantennas. This integration constructs micron-scale magnetophotonic crystals that produce sharp and narrow magneto-optical resonances, which can be precisely manipulated by both external magnetic fields and the incidence direction of incident light. The resulting narrow Fano-type resonance is generated by the coupling between inter-element surface plasmons of individual antennae and the Rayleigh anomalies of the collective antenna array; a computational framework grounded in Maxwell theory provides a complete explanation for this optical and magneto-optical mechanism. Ultimately, this stable magnetophotonic crystal establishes a platform for developing novel, high-symmetry optical directionality sensors and creating foundational structures for all-optical magnetization switching in ferrimagnetic RE-TM systems assisted by plasmonics.

We introduce VPN, a system designed for content attribution that recovers source history from redistributed video. Online, platforms and users typically alter video by modifying its quality, codec resolution, format, or aspect ratio, and may make minor adjustments like superimposing text or emojis. To address this, VPN learns a resilient search embedding capable of matching videos across these variations—including full-length clips and partial segments. After comparing against a database of verified clips, VPN returns the corresponding provenance data to the audience. The method employs contrastive learning to train a neural network for feature extraction using both raw and synthetic training data. Video is processed in inverted pairs (temporal chunks) using late-fusion to integrate visual and audio characteristics, enabling high-precision retrieval as demonstrated by test results on a dataset of 100,000 videos.

Measurements of the solar wind near 1 astronomical unit (au) indicate a predominantly outward radial flow, although there are instances where it deviates by as much as $15^\circ$ from radial, occurring in both east-west and north-south directions. East-west deflections frequently result from Stream Interaction Regions (SIRs). Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs) are implicated in non-radial flows in at least two ways: the deflection of the solar wind sheath boundary near the ejecta front, which can produce significant non-radial components, and the non-radial nature of the ejecta's expansion along non-central axes, which can easily be detected as one crosses the stream. This study reports on general statistical trends regarding these non-radial flows as detected by STEREO/PLASTIC over the mission's initial 13 years, with an emphasis on variations related to the solar cycle. By analyzing larger deflection angles, we find the majority occur at SIRs during solar minimum or in association with CMEs during solar maximum. Notably, we find little evidence for strongly deflected flows that one might anticipate from significant deflections alongside magnetic ejecta or ejecta possessing highly eccentric, elliptical cross-sections. Leveraging these findings, we refine our understanding of CME expansion and magnetic ejecta while identifying existing deficiencies in our knowledge of CMEs.

This study introduces I\^oWave, a vocoder grounded in both forward and backward linear stochastic differential equations (SDEs). By solving this equation pair, the system utilizes two stochastic processes that operate in reverse: first mapping a target waveform distribution into a more tractable space, and later reconstructing the realistic waveform from that simplified signal using initial conditional mel spectrograms. The It\^oS process acts on an additive Gaussian noise, driven by a Wiener process which progressively deducts the superimposed noise to recreate the signal across different latencies. Comparative experiments indicate that this model significantly improves upon the current state-of-the-art, achieving a predicted Mean Opinion Score (MOS) ranging between 4.32 and 4.39, with an average score of 4.35. Comprehensive examples of synthesized audio produced by this model are accessible via the associated repository link.

This study focuses on model-based multi-agent reinforcement learning within scenarios where environment transitions are unknown and must be learned through costly interactions. We introduce H-MARL (Hallucinated Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning), an innovative, sample-efficient framework designed to effectively balance exploration—understanding the environment—with exploitation, defined as attaining high-quality equilibrium outcomes in general-sum Markov games. H-MARL establishes rigorous high-probability confidence intervals around the uncertain transition model and iteratively refines them using fresh observational data. These intervals inform an optimistic "hallucinated" game for the agents to solve for optimal equilibrium policies in each round. The method accommodates general statistical frameworks (such as Gaussian processes or deep ensembles) and flexible policy architectures like deep neural networks, featuring theoretical analysis via bounds on agents' dynamic regret as well as convergence guarantees to the Markov game equilibrium. Experimental validation on autonomous driving benchmarks confirms that H-MARL rapidly learns successful equilibrium policies with minimal data interactions and outperforms non-optimistic exploratory strategies.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) are widely deployed within Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS), yet their complex nature introduces novel hazards that pose severe threats, necessitating robust strategies for building trustworthy systems. While DNNs deliver sophisticated performance, their successful integration into CPS relies on combining these models with solid engineering practices. This paper introduces an assurance monitoring approach for learning-based CPS derived from the conformal prediction framework. Real-time monitoring is enabled by utilizing distance learning to convert high-dimensional inputs into reduced-size embeddings. By applying conformal prediction, this method delivers well-calibrated confidence measures, guarantees a bound on the error rate, and constrains the frequency of inputs where accurate predictions cannot be achieved. The approach's efficacy is demonstrated across three datasets covering mobile robot wall-following, speaker recognition, and traffic sign recognition. Experimental findings confirm that the produced error rates are well-calibrated with minimal alarm generation, while also highlighting the method's computational efficiency and suitability for real-time CPS assurance monitoring.

Unsupervised progress has accelerated recently, particularly driven by contrastive self-supervised techniques. ImageNet has remained the primary benchmark, where recent approaches now rival those of fully supervised models; yet, because ImageNet is heavily object-focused, the effectiveness of these methods remains uncertain in non-object-centric domains like digital pathology, which also presents unique challenges. While self-supervised methods have shown promise there, the discrepancies between histopathology and natural imagery warrant further scrutiny. This paper offers an exhaustive analysis of contrastive learning applied to digital pathology, highlighting how the objective's performance shifts due to unique data traits. Key factors such as how views are generated for contrastive training and hyper-parameter adjustments are examined through a comprehensive series of experiments to assess impacts on tissue classification. Findings suggest a potential reduction in annotated data requirements for pathology, though success depends on adapting to specific data characteristics by fine-tuning view generation protocols and hyper-parameters. DevOps has evolved into one of the most influential paradigms in software engineering; nevertheless, its widespread adoption complicates the simultaneous achievement of secure software delivery and operational agility. This difficulty prompted a shift toward the DevSecOps approach—an emerging model of integrating security throughout the Dev lifecycle—that has attracted substantial attention in both industry and academia. Despite this interest, effectively implementing DevSecOps in real-world environments remains difficult. This study aims to organize existing insights into obstacles encountered by professionals adopting DevSecOps and to synthesize literature-based remedies. Additionally, the research identifies areas requiring further investigation. Employing Systematic Literature Review (SLR) of 54 peer-reviewed articles and applying thematic analysis, the study extracted patterns and relationships from the data. Results revealed 21 distinct adoption challenges paired with 31 proposed solutions. These findings, cross-evaluated to highlight research gaps, were grouped under four core themes: People, Practices, Tools, and Infrastructure. Most notably, data-driven friction points revolve around automation, making Tool challenges and solutions the most cited. Furthermore, "Security Shift-Left" methodologies and continuous assessment protocols were identified as pivotal DevSecOps habits that demand improvement. Moving forward, a dedicated focus must be placed on developer-centric security tools capable of supporting these continuous practices, alongside expanding research into automating legacy security manual tasks within fast paced delivery pipelines. Ultimately, practitioners still grapple with maintaining equilibrium between rapid release cycles and comprehensive security coverage.

Humor acts as a powerful element in routine human interaction and discourse, and computational humor modeling equips natural language processing (NLP) systems with the ability to amuse and connect with users. This study explores using a cutting-edge transfer learning technique for NLP, known as "prompting," specifically for identifying humor. Our findings indicate that while prompting achieves results comparable to fine-tuning when ample annotated data exists, it shines in resource-constrained scenarios for humor recognition. Additionally, we utilize sensitivity functions to dissect the connection between humor and offense; results reveal that such models may lean on offensive content to classify humor when performing this transfer task.

Many fluid dynamics finite element approaches depend on the streamline upwind Petrov-Galerkin (SUPG) term, weighted by a factor known as $\tau_{\mathrm{SUPG}}$. However, the standard calculation of $\tau_{\mathrm{SUPG}}$ incorporates a constant tied to the time step $\tau$, which breaks consistency when the time step becomes very small. Addressing this limitation, we suggest the "Consistent method," featuring a revised definition of $\tau_{\mathrm{SUPG}}$. Building upon the SUPG/PSPG framework, our strategy substitutes the explicit time step with a derived physics-based quantity formed by dividing the square norm of acceleration by velocity. We validate this proposal through three scenarios: steady pipe flow, fluid dynamics across a square block, and blood circulation within a patient-specific model. Results demonstrate that unlike existing approaches, our formulation maintains accuracy independent of step size; yet, the new system possesses greater numerical stiness that lowers the linear solver's convergence speed by up to tenfold significantly. In specific cases of steady pipe flow where an exact analytical benchmark exists, the proposed method achieves error reductions of as much as 99.8 percent at high Reynolds number conditions and small time step sizes.

Our experiments demonstrate clear superiority of the model against existing methods in both efficacy and speed.

Search-based procedural content generation (PCG) is an established technique for game level design, renowned for its generality and capacity to meet functional constraints. Nevertheless, the substantial computational expenses involved in running these algorithms in real-time have led to limited immediate adoption for in-game generation. This paper proposes the introduction of "mutation models," a novel iterative generation framework powered by machine learning. The core approach involves training a system to replicate evolutionary behaviors; during deployment, this trained entity sequentially corrects flawed input scenarios to produce refined levels, all while operating independently of a live fitness function. We tested these learned models across a 2D maze creation benchmark, comparing strategies where models utilized either only terminal evolution data or training checkpoints taken every 100 generations to evolve as a mutation operator itself. The "assisted evolution" strategy yielded superior results: resulting models generated valid puzzles at a 99.4 percent success rate against a high-diversity metric of 86 percent. Furthermore, these trained models operate orders of magnitude faster than the original evolutionary algorithms that produced them. This research paves the way for a paradigm shift in creating automatically learned level designers informed by evolutionary goals, offering tools with programmable constraints that achieve the speed required for real-time game integration.

We examine $f_{k}$, a time-averager serving as an estimator for a functional dependent on a Markov chain. Given specific conditions, $\hat f_{k}$ can be constructed without precomputation and, asymptotically, performs at least as efficiently as $f_{k}$ with a relative error factor approaching $1$. Furthermore, this framework yields an unbiased estimator for the bias inherent to $f_{k}$. Addressing this gap, we introduce a pixel-aware deep function-mixture network. This model relies on novel "Function-Mixture" (FM) blocks, each integrating basis functions—implemented as parallel subnetworks utilizing diverse receptive fields—and an auxiliary subnet acting as a mixing mechanism. This extra subnet generates pixel-level weights to linearly combine outputs from these bases, effectively determining the most appropriate field size and mapping strategy on a pixel-by-pixel basis for feature recovery and classification purposes. By layering multiple FM blocks, the architecture gains heightened flexibility in modeling these localized functions. Additionally, to facilitate efficient feature utilization and reduce computational costs while improving performance, intermediate features extracted from FB layers are integrated in later stages. Evaluations across three standard hyperspectral datasets demonstrate that this method significantly surpasses existing approaches in spectral resolution capabilities and robustness against noise, establishing its superiority for this task under various scenarios such as different illumination levels, motion blur conditions, and camera resolutions.

The puzzle game 2048 centers on combining tiles bearing powers of 2 to create larger ones; related versions utilize this merge mechanic for different numerical sequences.
