The existence and stability of collisionless, self-gravitating systems represent enduring challenges dating to D. Lynden-Bell's early research on violent relaxation and extending to dark matter (DM) halo virialization. A key outcome of this relaxation is that spherical equilibrium states, upon maximizing the entropy of the coarse-grained system, follow a Fermi-Dirac phase-space distribution. For DM fermions, this yields broad degenerate solutions featuring a compact degenerate core surrounded by an extended diffuse halo. Recent findings indicate that such halos can account for observed galaxy rotation curves, with their central core effectively simulating a black hole. However, a remaining uncertainty concerns whether these core-halo configurations can actually arise and persist stably over cosmological epochs. Our thermodynamic stability analysis, conducted within a cosmological microcanonical framework with fixed particle count at halo virialization, shows for the first time that these core-halo DM profiles are stable (representing entropy maxima) and possess extremely-long lifespans. Furthermore, we identify a critical instability threshold leading beyond which the dark matter core undergoes a catastrophic collapse into a supermassive black hole. Specifically, keV-range fermion particles only undergo such core collapse in virialized halos where the mass exceeds $10^9 M_\odot$ and formation redshift drops near 10 under our cosmology. Consequently, our findings confirm that non-linear structure formation can plausibly produce DM halos exhibiting a core-halo morphology.

Given the growing prevalence of multi-band systems with low-energy excitation, this study examines transport dynamics using the Boltzmann approach within a weakly disordered, non-interacting crystal containing multiple bands under a weak electric field. Typically, such multiband configurations significantly complicate Boltzmann solutions: even accounting solely for elastic impurity scattering, determining "dressed" velocities—one calculation required for every momentum state and band—is computationally intensive. This work introduces a semianalytical solution that streamlines this daunting numerical challenge into the much more manageable computation of a compact tensor; its specific size is determined merely by the number of occupied bands at the Fermi level. Building on this method, the paper also explores the interaction between symmetry and disorder regarding diverse impurity sources, including those derived from random-matrix Wigner distributions. Applying the approach to two-dimensional isotropic Rashba metals, the analysis fully characterizes in an analytical manner how various disorder types exacerbate transport anisotropy while violating the relaxation-time approximation, thereby enabling the detection of spin-orbit coupling signatures through anomalies in conductivity predictions based purely on Drude theory.

This study examines how strong interactions influence dressed energy levels within two-level systems. In scenarios dominated by strong dipole-dipole interactions, specific coupling patterns between these collective dressed states produce distinct sidebands in the fluorescence spectrum, a phenomenon heavily contingent upon spatial atomic arrangement. These couplings dictate both the prevalence of sidebands present in the spectrum and the distribution of the related energy frequencies. We detail a general approach for deriving dressed energy levels in any number of strongly interacting atoms, applying this method to two distinct spatial configurations of three-level systems; our results confirm that each arrangement yields unique coupled level dynamics, distinct primary energies, and varying numbers of observable sidebands, thereby allowing the fluorescence spectrum of such arrays to encode critical information regarding the count and configuration of the emitting particles.

Grasping the varied functions individuals play in facilitating large-scale information dissemination is crucial for regulating online conduct and its potential real-world ramifications. Consequently, most current research across various disciplines emphasizes the outsized impact attributed to highly interconnected "hub" nodes. Conversely, this work demonstrates that modeling information dissemination within online social networks achieves superior accuracy when it simultaneously extracts two distinct individual-level behavioral traits: influence propensities and susceptibility to new information. To this effect, we developed a nonlinear network-driven algorithm that calculates these specific influence measures using historical spreading event data. When this methodology was applied to substantial datasets spanning Twitter and Weibo, it revealed that an interdependent understanding of influence and susceptibility constitutes the primary drivers behind peer-to-peer information diffusion; omitting either metric significantly degrades prediction quality. Furthermore, our findings confirm that jointly analyzing these two attributes is necessary to precisely identify superspreaders, thereby contesting widespread assumptions regarding influential individuals in social networks.

We propose a novel "Absolute-relative" learning framework that leverages full label information to refine image representations and adjust the understanding of relations across both supervised and unsupervised domains, demonstrating performance improvements over current leading methods on public datasets.

Modern statistical applications frequently deal with high-dimensional datasets, making feature variable selection critical to scientific advancement. A key limitation remains, however: existing procedures often fail to adequately address data with heavy-tailed distributions, a defining trait of contemporary big data. Addressing this gap, our research introduces a Sure Screening method grounded in Robust Distance Correlation ("RDC") designed for heavy-tailed data in ultrahigh-dimensional regression. Our approach retains all beneficial attributes of standard distance correlation screening, including model independence, by also gaining significant benefits in robustly measuring association strength, thereby enhancing the overall effectiveness of feature screening. Extensive simulations across various scenarios confirm our procedure's superior performance in terms of feature detection, selection stability, and prediction accuracy compared to other established model-based and model-free techniques. Furthermore, application to The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) heavy-tailed RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data regarding pancreatic cancer demonstrates that RDC identifies biologically significant genes more effectively than competitor methods.

A novel all-optical method is introduced designed to enable ultrafast spin rotation, facilitating precise control over polarization in relativistic beam lines containing either lepton or ionized particles. Specifically, the technique employs single-pass interactions between co-traveling, relatively low-intensity laser fields—which are temporally asymmetric due to frequency chirping or sub-cycle THz characteristics—and dense, ultrashort beams of laser-generated matter. Through semi-classical numerical simulations, we determine that spin rotation in asymmetric laser environments can be flexibly regulated by adjusting the phase delay between spin precession and oscillatory momentum. Consequently, an initial proton beam polarization can be shifted to virtually any specific alignment, such as converting transverse to longitudinal polarization required for various applications, with high-fidelity results (precision exceeding 99%) on a femtosecond or tens-of-femtoseconds timescale using accessible frequency-chirped laser setups. Importantly, the procedure notably enhances beam properties by improving the energy spectrum and increasing energy resolution. Beyond fundamental research, this technique promises significant utility across multiple fields requiring ultrafast spin control, particularly in areas spanning atomic, molecular, laser-plasma physics, laser-nuclear physics, or high energy particle applications.

Leveraging designs originally intended for the ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (ATLASPix), AstroPix aims to preserve high-performance metrics and operate with low power and reduced noise, facilitated by dual-detection and readout functions across each pixel. A comprehensive overview of the current developmental status, experimental results, and prospective future applications of the AstroPixel technology.

Standard development practices typically start with the main execution flow and then address alternative scenarios and edge cases. However, many programs suffer from overlooked, irregular conditions that invoke unexpected behaviors which cannot be anticipated from existing specifications, leading to developers neglecting them. To solve this lacunar issue, we introduce the concept of "code sophistication," defined here as the detection and recommendation of omitted behaviors. In contrast to traditional coding assistance that generates suggestions based on defined intents to complete programs, code Sophistication operates where specifications lack, to enable the integration of requisite yet un-codèd behaviors. We delineate key challenges within this domain. This paper investigates matching theory in 5G non-cellular, heterogeneous mmWave networks, focusing on the method for users connecting in a distributed setting. We present a new, high-efficiency distributed algorithm called Early Acceptance (EA). This framework enables users, sorted by preference, to seek connection with their preferred base stations. If there remains unassigned quota in that preferred base station, they receive an offer immediately. These proposed EA mechanisms, various versions including manual preference updates for reapplying, are evaluated alongside the traditional Deferred Acceptance (DA) approach—standard for its maximum stability, where users await acceptance pending a finalized matching at each station. While matching yields acceptable stability, we demonstrate it should not necessarily ensure the best performance in throughput metrics. Analysis and data show a decisive edge for our Early Acceptancy approach: it outperforms the classic Deferred Approach by securing higher end-users throughputs all while significantly reducing system processing delay. Ultimately, whether run once or multiple times by its user base to hit equilibrium conditions, these Early Acceptancy games approximate the results achievable in an enterprise network model having such centralized control over user association and allowing much simpler, lower cognitive complexity processing.

A primary challenge in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) is effectively capturing the relevance of neighbor nodes during aggregation. Many GNN architectures address this by implicitly learning node importance weights, often labeled as implicit GNNs, with Graph attention Networks serving as a prominent instance. Fundamentally, these models operate by integrating specific graph properties into Learnable Transformation Structures (LTS), which utilize data-driven methods to weight neighboring nodes. This research contends, however, that LTS causes the unique characteristics of this graph information to dissolve during training, rendering the data ineffective for deriving node representations—a condition termed Graph Information Vanishing (GIV). Furthermore, it is demonstrated that LTS projects diverse graph information into nearly indistinguishable outcomes. We validate these two findings through two separate series of 70 randomized trials involving five implicit GNN models and seven datasets; notably, we employed random permutation to scramble data ordering. Results show that in 93% of instances, model performance was unaffected, with only 6-19 examples exhibiting a marginal accuracy drop. Additionally, calculated cosine similarities on output results across 81% of mappings exceeded 99%, indicating a high degree of homogeneity. Experimental outcomes substantiate the existence of GIV in current implicit GNN approaches, suggesting they fail to exploit graph information efficiently, thereby necessitating a re-evaluation of the interaction between graph data and LTS for improved node representations.

We define an $n$-length classical parking function of positive integers $(a_1, \ldots, a_n)$ such that its nondecreasing sequence $(b_1, \ldots, b_n)$ fulfills $b_i \leq i$. Its geometric characteristics were investigated by Amanbayeva and Wang (2022) following a query raised by Stanley (2020). This paper extends the study of such polytopes by analyzing $\mathbf{x}$-parking function polytopes—the convex hull of $\mathbf{x}$-parking functions where $\mathbf{x}=(a,b,\dots,b)$—and the relationships they share with partial permutahedra described by Heuer and Striker (2022) as well as the Pitman-Stanley polytopes. Notably, we derive a specific formula for calculating the volume of $\mathbf{x}$-parking function polytopes; doing so settles a conjecture by Behrend and colleagues (2022) and yields the initial closed-form volume expression for classical parking function convex hulls as a result.

We leverage spectroscopic data from the VANDELS survey integrated with a $\simeq$7 Ms Chandra Deep Field South survey region to investigate high-mass X-ray binary (XRB) systems across 301 normal star-forming galaxies at redshifts $3 < z < 5.5$. By conducting a redshift- and SFR-binned stacking analysis of sources with robust spectroscopic redshifts free from AGN contaminants, we identify clear evolutionary trends in the $L_X$/SFR ratio extending to the survey's red limits; notably, these trends are more pronounced in lower-SFR galaxies. Combining these findings with existing lower-redshift samples, we determine that the evolution of $L_X$/SFR approaching $z \simeq 5$ follows a scaling of $(1+z)^{1.03 \pm 0.02}$. Derived metal ratios confirm that even at higher redshifts, metal-poor galaxies exhibit higher $L_X$/SFR values compared to lower-$Z$ counterparts. Furthermore, by quantifying the redshift-dependent contribution of XRBs to the cosmic X-ray luminosity density and benchmarking our results against models, estimates for the contribution of high-mass XRBs to the cosmic X-ray background at $z > 6$ may exceed prior values by $\gtrsim 0.25$ dex.

The task of visual storytelling involves crafting engaging and appropriate narratives that align with given image sequences. In this study, our primary goal is to generate storylines that exhibit greater variety without losing the informative details present in the visuals. To achieve improved diversity alongside informativeness, we introduced a concept selection module capable of proposing multiple candidate concepts. Subsequently, a large-scale pre-trained model transforms these concepts and input images into comprehensive narratives. To broaden the pool of candidate concepts for each sequence, we construct a commonsense knowledge graph. To effectively select relevant concepts from this graph, we developed two novel modules that specifically address both the internal correlations among concepts and their relationships with the corresponding images. Robust evaluations conducted both automatically by algorithms and subjectively by humans confirm that our model generates highly viable concepts. Consequently, our approach substantially outperforms earlier methods in terms of both story diversity and informative content generation, while maintaining the narrative relevance to the source image sequence.

Recent research demonstrates that Binarized Neural Networks (BNNs) significantly lower computational expenses and memory requirements, thereby aiding the deployment of models on hardware with limited resources. However, compared to their full-precision analogs, these binary networks typically experience substantial accuracy loss. Consequently, creating a robust strategy to binarize 1x1 layers is essential to enhance BNN utility. To address this, we introduce our "Elastic-Link" (EL) module, which enhances intra-network information flow by allowing real-valued inputs from previous convolutions to directly contribute to subsequent binary features. Designed for seamless integration and compatible with existing BNN methods, the proposed EL framework proves highly effective. Experimental results on large-scale datasets like ImageNet validate distinct improvements, such as increasing ResNet26's top-1 accuracy from 57.9% to 64.0% and facilitating training convergence for binarized MobileNet, reaching a top-1 accuracy of 56.4%. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) were designed to identify complex descriptors, such as textures and geometrical structures, to facilitate image recognition. Applying varied image styles during training has demonstrated reducing this textural dependency in favor of shape bias simultaneously enhancing robustness against common corruptions, thereby improving resilience to issues like blur or noise. We conducted a systematic investigation employing various input compositions utilizing natural images, edge representations, and stylization techniques. We introduce a universal explanation for the significant magnetic field effects observed in nonmagnetic organic semiconductors. A weak magnetic field, measured at less than hundreds of mT, can drastically alter the electron hopping rate between adjacent organic molecules when the magnetic length remains comparable to or is only moderately longer than both the molecular spacing and the electronic localization length. Illumination or a high electric field amplifies this by modifying the polaron density, rendering phenomena such as photocurrent, photoluminescence, electroluminescence, magnetoresistance, and electrically injected current sensitive to even weak fields. The proposed theory successfully accounts for all empirically observed features while establishing a rigorous foundational framework for existing phenomenological fitting models.

Although it is well-established that deep learning models are vulnerable to adversarial inputs, this susceptibility regarding image caption generation remains inadequately explored. Our research investigates adversarial techniques applied to vision-language models operating within an encoder-decoder architecture, which utilizes a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for image feature extraction and a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) for text synthesis. Specifically, we target the hidden layers within the visual encoder before they are transmitted to the recurrent network. Unlike existing approaches that either attack the visual encoder's final classification layer or propagate gradients from the language model backward, we introduce a GAN-based algorithm to generate adversarial samples for neural image captioning. This method mimics the CNN's internal representations, ensuring that the deep features extracted from the input image compel the subsequent recurrent network to produce specific, intentionally incorrect captions. Our analysis yields fresh perspectives on adversarial vulnerabilities in vision systems that include linguistic elements and involves two strategies: the ability of the image captioning framework to generate targeted deceptive outputs and the potential for embedding specific keywords within predicted text. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm successfully crafts adversarial images via perturbations in CNN hidden layers to mislead the entire captioning process. Furthermore, we find these attacks to be highly transferable, thereby introducing critical security implications for improving the robustness of neural image captioning systems.

Although literature aligns largely on the estimand and estimator definitions for the Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney (WMW) test, determining the most effective variance estimator remains ambiguous. This review not only assess various WMW approaches but also examines different variances that remain consistent under both null and alternative hypotheses. It additionally considers methods proposed by others for approximations that apply to scenarios with small sample sizes, including approaches using a t-distribution, logit transformations, and permutations. Various estimators were also investigated for determining the relevant degrees of freedom within t-based approximations, with simulated scenarios generating results indicating that performance differences between estimators were mostly reliant upon the specific patterns of heteroskedasticity used and the relative allocation ratios between samples, rather than on the specific distributions. Collectively, a specific t-based approximation combined with Perme's variance estimator continued to safeguard the nominal significance level best.

We introduce and analyze an adapted step-size modification to Davis-Yin's three-operator splitting method. This approach addresses optimization scenarios involving a smooth objective with a computable gradient and multiple non-smooth functions accessible via their proximal operators by determining step sizes using local objective data, thereby enabling significantly higher values. Furthermore, it necessitates only two additional function evaluations per iteration and eliminates the dependency on tunable step-size parameters beyond a starting guess. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that the method achieves an iteration complexity rate matching the leading non-adaptive results: it offers both the well-stated sublinear convergence applicable to all convex instances and linear convergence provided by the strong convexity of the smooth term plus one other proximal term. Finally, computational evidence derived from comparing related techniques across six distinct problems substantiates the method's efficiency advantages.

The Sun releases vast numbers of photons and neutrinos in an almost spatially symmetric pattern. Introducing $\gamma$-ray and ultra-high energy (UHE) neutrinos from distant galaxies leads to interactions—specifically annihilations—with these solar particles, a process driven by their subsequent collision. Such interaction-induced anisotropies in the diffuse $\gamma$-ray and solar flux stem from the attenuation of these backgrounds, a measurable effect serving as an effective lever for exploring the electroweak force. Our latest Letter evaluates these induced anisotropies, predicting values on Earth near $\simeq 1\times 10^{-16}\,(2\times 10^{-14})\%$ for TeV-scale $\gamma$-ray and respective scale UHE neutrinos attenuation respectively. We further assess promising observational avenues offered by experiments like the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope (Fermi) Large Area Satellite, HAWC (Hamburger Water Collection), and IceCube facilities. Further, there is also an opportunity in exploring the abilities of other satellites like the Parker Solar Observatory for capturing possible energy signals during its mission.

Current quantum compilers enhance quantum circuits through expert-defined circuit transformations. However, creating and deploying these transformations requires extensive manual effort to adapt to the varying gate sets of specific quantum devices and often results in missed optimizations due to the limitations of human effort alone. We introduce Quartz, an automated circuit superoptimizer capable of independently generating and verifying circuit transformations tailored to any quantum gate set. To this end, Quartz exploits small circuits via systematic exploration to propose candidate optimizations, which an automated theorem prover then validates. The optimization of arbitrary circuits is achieved through a backtracking search algorithm weighted by cost, applying these confirmed transformations. Evaluation across three prevalent gate sets demonstrates that Quartz successfully generates verified optimizations that either surpass those hand-engineered by current systems or reproduce their exact logic. Additionally, it introduces entirely novel transformations, enabling effective circuit optimization applicable to a wide spectrum of gate configurations.

This paper proposes Poisson mixture models tailored for origin-destination modeling within transportation studies. These models, built around covariates, span multiple transport modeling stages and facilitate direct Bayesian probabilistic inference of link traffic flows. The authors make the Poisson-inverse Gaussian the primary focus of this work by presenting its first complete Bayesian specification, positioning it effectively against traditional Poisson-gamma and Poisson-lognormal frameworks. The discussion underscores the Poisson-inverse Gaussian as a superior choice for origin-destination analyses by highlighting its advantageous marginal and hierarchical characteristics. Furthermore, an integrated nested Laplace approximation (INLA) approach is explored alongside Markov chain Monte Carlo methods, including a comparative analysis grounded in stated assumptions. To demonstrate these techniques, a case study utilizing 2001 Belgian census data is employed, examining the trip volumes in 308 Flemish municipalities within expansive, sparsely populated matrices derived for origin-destination research purposes.

This paper investigates a single machine scheduling scenario aiming to reduce the sum of completion times, where jobs are categorized as either "short" or "long," though their specific processing durations are initially unknown. The availability of this hidden information relies on a probability oracle accessed via execution, where each test incurs a cost of one time unit; thus, algorithms must determine how to query job processing times efficiently. The performance of the generated schedule is evaluated against an ideal optimal schedule that possesses complete information, using the derived Competitive ratio to quantify this uncertainty. The research concentrates on two frameworks: a non-adaptive setting, where the selection between testing a job and executing an untested one is fixed in advance, and an adaptive framework, allowing dynamic decision-making in response to prior test results. We propose optimal polynomial-time solutions for both scenarios utilizing a two-stage method: a preliminary testing phase, followed immediately by an oblivionsally-execution phase of the remaining jobs. Experimental findings robustly indicate the superiority of this structured approach, whereas a theoretical proof of this universal structure remains an unresolved challenge.

In contexts requiring significant environment exploration despite scarce external rewards for the learning agent, curiosity offers effective intrinsic incentives to facilitate discovery of necessary goal-oriented knowledge. While current models demonstrate high utility across rare-reward situations, they often treat state sequences too generically without capturing fine-grained environmental details or structure. Our approach recasts curiosity as a form of question-anchored inquiry, driven by motivating agents to pose environmental questions and detecting shifts in their corresponding responses. We report that forming natural language queries compels the discovery of distinct contextual data—including object physical characteristics and spatial dynamics—which function as robust intrinsic rewards for more effectively tackling low-reward objectives.

This study focuses on the automated reconciliation of receivables within non-governmental organizations by employing entity matching techniques. We examine a workflow utilizing a baseline algorithm for initial match ranking, which is then refined through several newly proposed methods—including score post-processing, a cascade model, and a chain model—to enhance overall accuracy. These contributions advance the fields of automated reconciliation, entity matching, and multilabel classification in open-ended scenarios. Tested on operational data from a firm offering reconciliation-as-a-service, the framework successfully elevates the recall rate from 78% (the performance of the base model) to over 90% while maintaining 99% precision.

The sampling-based planning evaluation suite, known as "sbp-env," represents a comprehensive platform designed for the rapid testing of diverse sampling-based motion planning algorithms, emphasizing flexibility and the ease of adjusting various configuration aspects. To achieve this modular adaptability, the architecture separates primary planning elements into two distinct categories: (i) samplers and (ii) planner algorithms, aligning these divisions with the core focus of current research. This paper applies established Bayesian probabilistic methods from signal analysis to the task of determining air bubble radii beneath the surface. We present the bubblegram, a feature extraction method analogous in display to the spectrogram but engineered to isolate only those pulses aligning with a specific physical model. We introduce Lossy Implicit Network Activation Coding (LINAC), a novel defensive strategy that transforms inputs to counter various common adversarial attacks against CIFAR-$10$ classifiers. Specifically, LINAC remains effective for perturbations with an $L_\infty$ norm of $\epsilon = 8/255$ and an $L_2$ norm of $\epsilon = 0.5$. We identify the random seed initializing the implicit neural representation as critical information, effectively serving as a "private key" that enables more powerful generic attacks in an effort to compromise the defense. In response, we developed a new attack methodology called the Parametric Bypass Approximation (PBA), designed to undermine existing key-based defenses; while our PBA successfully invalidated another such method, linaci also mitigates various transfer and adaptive attacks, including our own proposed strategy for bypassing the key-based defense and those utilizing the PBA approach. Collectively, our results highlight the vital need to evaluate defenses across a wide spectrum of customised attacks, despite the system likely demonstrating robustness in standard metrics. The mechanisms by which real-world happenings impact the nature and sentiment of online discourse remain incompletely explored. Robot learning represents a vital area for advancing the future of automation and artificial intelligence. The goal for upcoming robotic systems is to function autonomously by mastering fundamental skills, constructing cognitive representations of their surroundings, and engaging with them dynamically. Although simulation environments have addressed these issues extensively, practical robot learning research remains notably constrained. Real-world applications face specific obstacles, including sensor noise, actuator inaccuracies, the necessity of safe exploration, shifting environmental dynamics, the complexities of autonomous resetting, and prohibitive long-duration experiment costs. Without scalable solutions to overcome these hurdles, the realization of complex, contact-rich tasks—particularly those requiring fine hand-eye coordination—will likely remain a distant dream confined strictly to controlled laboratory settings. To address this, we propose dual-robot configurations as viable platforms for machine learning. These setups facilitate robust data gathering for skill development and perceptual training in a supervised manner, while simultaneously simplifying environment recovery. Moreover, by incorporating adversarial learning grounded in game theory, we can maximize exploration strategies and ensure safety through collaborative constraints; consequently, the models exhibit superior generalization capabilities. Finally, we will examine the inherent benefits, existing challenges, and potential research trajectories offered by such dual-arm systems.

Love waves propagate across the boundary of heterogeneous media as antiplane elastic waves. Operating under time-harmonic conditions, these waves obey a Helmholtz-type scalar equation to which arbitrary planar coordinate transformations leave it invariant, a property leveraged in the design of broad-band surface- defect cloaks specifically utilizing transformation elastodynamics. We calculated the required isotropic, spatially varying elastic characteristics to perfectly mask triangular and parabolic anomalies. To verify this framework, we employed both dispersion theories and time-frequency harmonic numerics, subsequently constructing practical cloak models using layered materials of monosomic construction with homogenized metrics fitting the ideal parameters. Validation through second-kind simulations confirms that these fabricated structures achieve considerable attenuation of waves scattered from embedded flaws.

We hypothesize that vigorous convection triggered by a core helium flash in low-mass red giant branch (RBG) stars generates waves propagating into the envelope, with the deposited energy driving envelope expansion and increased brightness. Drawing energy estimates and mechanistic assumptions from prior studies on massive stars experiencing core convection prior to core-collapse supernovae, our simulation code MESA reveals that waves can expand the envelope by tens to hundreds of solar radii within just a few years. Although this phase entails significant brightening, the concurrent growth in radius and luminosity markedly enhances dust production and the mass loss rate. These processes shift stellar emissions deeper into infrared frequencies and may dim visible brightness, resulting in an observed signature of faint, red transient activity lasting months to a few years. Furthermore, we propose that such envelope expansion around pre-evolved RGB stars enables the survival of several Jupiter-mass exoplanets and higher-mass free-floating planetary objects—such as brown dwarfs—even as their host encounters common envelope phases, by reducing the system's gravitational binding energy. This model offers an explanation for the planetary system surrounding the white dwarf WD1856+534 and the white dwarf–brown dwarf pairing found in ZTFJ003855.0+203025.5.

Assessing and designing future experimental efforts heavily depends on forecasting the scientific returns of potential measurements. The Fisher information matrix is frequently utilized for this purpose because of its favorable mathematical characteristics and efficiency; however, it serves merely as a reasonable estimate of the true likelihood function under assumptions of approximately Gaussian-distributed data and nearly linear parameter dependencies in observables. Moreover, Fisher forecasting methods inherently cannot evaluate their own applicability. While exhaustive sampling of the precise or synthetic likelihood offers a definitive test of Fisher forecast validity, it is often computationally unfeasible. This study presents a straightforward method, grounded in the Derivative Approximation for Likelihoods (DALI), to verify whether the Fisher matrix adequately replicates the true likelihood. We establish that when two-dimensional cuts along level curves derived from DALI show negative extrinsic curvature, the Fisher approximation deteriorates. Furthermore, our results confirm that this detection approach reliably identifies deviations between Fisher forecasts and actual likelihood behavior across diverse cosmological scenarios and datasets, all while incuring only a minimal computational overhead compared to conventional Fisher forecasts.

Sixth-generation (6G) wireless technology will utilize an architecture encompassing "space, air, ground, and sea." OoT devices are capable not only of gathering information underwater but also of facilitating communication via airborne radio frequencies. While Underwater Acoustic Communication (UWA COMMs) is currently the most effective medium for these devices, it faces persistent issues regarding Doppler shifts and synchronization errors. Addressing these difficult underwater communication conditions, this paper introduces C-DNN, a deep neural network-based receiver for acoustic chirp communications. Furthermore, to enhance deep learning model performance and mitigate generalization challenges, a novel Federated Meta-Learning (FML)-augmented Acoustic-Radio Cooperative (ARC) framework, named ARC/FML, is proposed. The study derives analytically tractable expressions to evaluate the convergence rate of FML in wireless environments, specifically considering individual node data volume, the number of local iterations, and scheduling ratios. Analytical results alongside simulations demonstrate that the C-DNN receiver offers superior bit error rate performance and reduced computational complexity compared to classical matched filter approaches for UWA scenarios. Additionally, the ARC/FML framework achieves convergence performance across diverse channels that surpasses standard Federated Learning. In conclusion, the proposed OoT-based ARC/FML scheme presents a promising solution for exchanging information across both air and water media.

Although new words frequently enter social groups, they do not all remain in use. While several factors drive changes in vocabulary, this research highlights the relatively overlooked influence of social networks. By examining more than 80,000 neologisms across 4,420 online communities over a ten-year period using Poisson regression and survival analysis, our study shows that network topology substantially impacts word adoption. Factors beyond total size—specifically dense interconnectivity, low local clustering, and numerous external ties—foster both the introduction and survival of new terms. Distinct from face-to-face gatherings—which resist widespread leveling despite high contact—even though these online, topic-specific groups show minimal lexical leveling, they successfully accommodate niche vocabulary. Thus, our findings validate the sociolinguistic theory that network structures influence lexical evolution while also providing unique, data-backed insights relevant to internet environments.

Network embeddings, though extensively researched and widely applied to tasks such as link prediction and node classification, have seen previous works prioritize novel algorithms or topic-specific adaptations while neglecting the critical role of learning initialization strategies. This study targets that overlooked gap, demonstrating that optimized initialization can substantially enhance algorithmic effectiveness and efficiency. Specifically, our method employs graph partitioning to divide the network into disconnected subsets and creates a representative, reduced-scale conceptual graph. We derive initial node embeddings for this smaller abstract model through existing network embedding processes, then propagate these vectors to individual node embeddings. Extensive experiments reveal this initialization approach boosts the performance of top-tier algorithms by up to 8.74% in classification and 7.76% in link prediction. Furthermore, the proposed technique cuts execution time for state-of-the-art algorithms by at least 20%.

Knowledge Graphs, which underpin technologies ranging from recommender engines to corporate knowledge management and Open Data, function by assembling information needs through interconnected chains of small data units called triples. However, data curators often face the challenge of manually reconstructing these trios, a high-cognitive process that obstructs their ability to effectively survey their datasets. This paper presents "path outlines"—statistical conceptual representations that characterize sequences of triples. Based on evaluations from 11 data producers, we introduce the Path Outlines tool, which utilizes coordinated views and two novel visualization techniques to facilitate browsing of such path summaries. Experimental comparisons against baseline methods with 36 participants reveal that Path Outlines triple the speed of data exploration, improve task completion, reduce errors, and are preferred by participants for its intuitiveness in making complex tasks easier.

This paper introduces a method to efficiently retrieve high-fidelity, clean CAD models from extensive databases for the purpose of recovering detailed geometries from RGBD scans. Contrary to prior approaches that merely rank objects using shape descriptors on a limited database by selecting the top result only, our hypothesis is that larger databases benefit from exploring the descriptor neighborhood to identify more accurate matches. Crucially, we propose compensating for the specificity limitations of instance-level shape descriptors by employing geometry-based re-ranking of the retrieved neighborhood. The proposed pipeline first utilizes the discriminant capabilities of learned features to categorize model types and subsequently applies a newly introduced robust point set distance metric to refine neighbors within those categories. This combination enables precise, fine-grained retrieval across a large-scale shape library. Performance evaluation confirms that our method offers a simple yet highly efficient re-ranking strategy, yielding a substantial boost in accuracy over existing state-of-the-art techniques when tested on real-world datasets.

Given the arduous process traditionally involved in manually creating detailed discourse trees, we simultaneously present a technique for scaling corpus size and preserving diversity within treebanks. Consequently, our study applies these inferred general tree structures across multiple linguistic domains, exhibiting strong performance on a variety of related tasks.

Delay Tolerant Networking (DTN) is a framework engineered to address communication challenges such as significant latency and network outages found across diverse network types. Replicating these real-world networking architectures and protocols is often challenging due to their inherent complexity; thus, this document outlines Urban Delay Tolerant Network Simulator (UTDN Sim) v 0.1. This simulator replicates urban roadway settings exhibiting key DTN properties like specific routing protocols and motion behaviors. The current iteration includes six mobility models: Stationary Movement, Simple Random Movement, Path Type-Based Motion, Path Memory-Based Motion, Path Type with Restricted Movement, and Path Type with Wait Motion. The toolkit further encompasses three routing and data transfer mechanisms: Epidemic Routing, Superior Only Offloading (OH), and Superior Peer Hand-off. Built via object‑oriented design to ensure extensible features, UTDSim v 0.1 is available as an open-source simulator to benefit research efforts globally.

Recent breakthroughs in meta-learning have achieved exceptional outcomes on various few-shot learning benchmarks. Nevertheless, this success frequently neglects the alignment between training and test tasks, creating the possibility of evaluation bias. Consequently, we introduce a generative model built on a variant of Latent Dirichlet Examination to assess task similarity, thereby optimizing and clarifying meta-learning performance. Our findings reveal that this approach yields an enlightening assessment on two few-shot classification benchmarks that aligns with established logic: greater task similarity corresponds to superior performance. Utilizing this similarity metric, we devise a strategy for task selection that outperforms random task selection by generating more accurate classification results.

The upper critical dimension for standard critical behavior in the Ising model was historically understood by many to be four ($d_{c}=4$). From our results, we conclude that based on cluster models (in its random-cluster picture), its new upper critical dimensions at $2 = {4;6}$; it appears as another special physical case for dimensions $4 + $ where its properties were identified as percolating per unit. We predict there could be multiple dimensions per unit and support our claims with simulation data from graphs ranging from 4-7 per unit, including complete case-graph examples that are known in physics literature today.

Non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) remains a common technique for extracting low-dimensional data features; however, it treats every attribute equally, resulting in representations that may lack accuracy. Take, for instance, a set of face images: if the subject is wearing a hat, ideal analysis should discount or remove the visual emphasis on that specific attribute. To tackle this limitation, we introduce entropy-weighted NMF (EWNMF), a novel variant that employs learnable weights to adjust the significance assigned to individual attributes. We achieve this by appending an entropy regularization term to the objective function and resolving the resulting constraints via the Lagrange multiplier method. Experiments across multiple benchmarks validate both the viability and performance of our approach. The implementation code is hosted at https://github.com/Poisson-EM/Entropy-weighted-NMF.

HEALPix, or Hierarchical Equal Area isoLatitude Pixelization, serves as an established tool in both high-energy physics and gravitational research within the field astronomy. Although it was first designed to enhance the efficiency of computing full skies Fourier maps, it has also been adopted for communicating sky location data across a broad community. A significant challenge to wider acceptance lies in its requirement for a uniform all-sky grid. To address this constraint, we present `mhealpy`, an adaptable Python framework developed for the creation, management, evaluation and visualization multi-resolution maps, enabling high-fidelity sky coverage. The library not only allows for rapid access, operations between datasets and flexible image file conversion (`.fits`), but it can also dynamically adjust or "zoomed" resolution for concentrated regions, promoting its success on shared multi-resolution maps and effective multi-sensor analysis.

We introduce a new sound localization technique for indoor environments where the sound source is not in direct line of sight (NLOS). Our method leverages the way sound waves bend, known as diffraction, when encountering obstacles or barriers within a scene. By merging a ray tracing sound propagation model with Uniform Theory of Diffraction (UTD)—which models this bending effect through virtual sound sources placed on edges—we precompute diffraction wedges from a reconstructed 3D mesh of indoor settings. Predicting theoretical band offsets at interfaces within semiconductor heterostructures is frequently difficult. While density functional theory has proven quite effective for such computations, there is a desire for efficient and precise semilocal functionals that lower computational expenses; typically, GGA-based semilocal functionals overly reduce bulk band gaps, leading to inaccurate band offset estimations for these interfaces. This study evaluates several sophisticated meta-GGA functionals for predicting band offsets at semiconductor heterojunctions, specifically examining r2SCAN, rMGGAC, mTASK, and LMBJ exchange–correlation potentials. Findings indicate that these meta-GGA approaches perform remarkably well in supercell calculations relative to the significantly costlier GW method. Furthermore, we provide results for both charge-density alignment methods—band offsets derived from ionization potentials/electron affinities and alignment via branch-point energies—to complement directly computed quantities. Collectively, these results confirm that the listed meta-GGA frameworks are viable tools under DFT for estimating semiconductor band offsets with high predictive reliability in heterostructures.

Device-Independent Quantum Key Distribution (DI-QKD) represents the pinnacle of secure communication by allowing for verified key exchange using uncertalised black-box equipment. This approach successfully addresses numerous loopholes and side channels affecting existing quantum key distribution schemes. While practical implementation remains technically difficult, advancing both experimental capabilities and theoretical frameworks has enabled several recent proof-of-principle tests. This review introduces fundamentals of DI-QKD, examines related experimental efforts, details the theories and analysis techniques necessary to validate its security, and concludes with a discussion on prospective directions for future research.

We posit that a process involving the bifurcation of a fuzzy space offers an explanation for both the origin of black hole entropy and the apparent validity of a "generalized second law of thermodynamics" within black hole physics. By analyzing microstates in a model where the black hole is represented as fuzzy space, our approach recovers the Bekenstein-Hawking formula, resulting in a discrete area spectrum. Specifically, as the black hole approaches the Planck scale, the spacing between these area eigenvalues increases. Consequently, our analysis indicates that as the black hole evaporates becomes increasingly entropically depleted; this evolution suggests that certain information concerning the black hole's primordial state may be recoverable.

Estimating 3D human poses from single-view images poses significant challenges as an inherently ill-posed task driven by shadows and occlusions. Yet, most incumbent research disregards these uncertainties, opting instead for singular solutions. In opposition to this approach, our method produces a varied array of hypotheses capable of modeling the comprehensive posterior distribution of valid 3D poses. Specifically, this involves introducing a normalizing flow framework leveraging its deterministic forward projection (from 3D to 2D) to address the cumbersome reversibility of the mapping (from 2D to 3D). Moreover, uncertainty in feature localization is accurately modeled within an integrated 3D pose prior adapted with joint 3D constraint techniques known to the global optimization problem via maximum a posteriori (MAP). Finally, our method has achieved encouraging results with high consistency across all benchmark datasets. Source code can be downloaded from the accompanying GitHub repository.

While building upon the simplicity of well-established Relativistic Mean-Field (RMF) theory, the NLD model introduces field-theoretical momentum dependencies. These results are critical for forthcoming experiments such as those planned at CBM, the PANDA facility within FAIR, and hold significant relevance for nuclear astrophysics.

The dramatic increase in Internet users in recent years has generated a vast volume of unstructured data, primarily in the form of social media text within health communities. A substantial portion of these individuals is active in health-related social networks sharing medical insights. To address this pressing issue, this paper examines the sentiments and emotions expressed by users about their specific medical conditions through their posts on popular platforms. We utilized major medical discussion boards, namely *Patient.info* and *dailystrength.org*, to analyze discussions surrounding critical health issues such as depression, anxiety, allergy, and asthma. First, a benchmark framework was established after collecting the data; this included the definition of fine-grained sentiment labels corresponding to medical statuses: "Recovered," "Present" (Exist), "Worsening" (Deteriorate), and "Other" conditions. We developed a novel architectural approach combining a Support Vector Machine (SVM) for classification with a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), used here as a data-driven feature extraction method. Furthermore, a context-aware sentiment feature was crafted specifically to interpret emotions within medical contexts, which was shown to boost the model's accuracy beyond feature extraction alone when employed jointly. Beyond our primary dataset, the proposed method's efficacy was confirmed against the "CLEF eHealth 2014" benchmark corpus, demonstrating that it achieves superior results compared with state-of-the-art solutions.

Learning directly from unprocessed input data reduces reliance on manual feature engineering and forms a foundational aspect of successfulMachine learning across many domains. While many issues easily adapt to vector formats suitable for standard classifiers, various data sources naturally occur as structured interchange formats (such as security logs in JSON or XML); however, few methods address learning from this raw structure efficiently. Existing approaches like Hierarchical Multiple Instance Learning (HMIL) enable such processing yet overlook the interpretability of models trained in this way. By framing these problems as subset selection challenges, we showcase computationally efficient algorithms that generate explanations for raw-structured models possessing commendable qualities. Our approach outperforms prevailing explanation techniques borrowed from graph neural networks by an order of magnitude in both speed and the caliber of produced interpretations.

In this study, we discuss recent advances in establishing cyclic cocycles within the Harish-Chandra Schwartz algebra for a simply connected reductive real Lie group \(G\) and explore their relevance to elevated index theory concerning proper, cocompact group actions.

A new digital analyzer has been created for measuring the mechanical tension across groups of wires with specified length and density, as well as assessing both electrical continuity and isolation. The system determines wire tension by capturing its resonant frequencies—specifically, the fundamental frequency which changes with tension magnitude. The instrument functions by applying direct high voltage between adjacent wires, then introducing a variable alternating high voltage while monitoring resonance in the center wire. An automated process tests up to 128 wires, reading data from eight at a time. The resulting digital wire analyzer (DWA) offers 1% precision in tension measurements, achieving this through tuning detection when the operating frequency aligns precisely with the fundemental frequency of each wire.

We introduce a comprehensive global examination of the Higgs mechanism and electroweak sector utilizing the Effective Field Framework; this study incorporates functional method-matching techniques within the Standard Model Effective Field Framework to a specific New Physics extension, namely, the electroweak gauge-trlet triplet scenario. Working within the SFitter framework at one loop level and addressing the resultant UV-model matching explicitly, our analysis emphasizes minimizing and accounting for corresponding theoretical uncertainties. We show how SMEFT and model-specific analyses complement one another within these confines.

We apply the techniques of Bragg spectroscopy to a light fluid under paraxial conditions using wavefront shaping with spatial light modulators, specifically imprinting analogues of short-duration light pulses onto it. By analyzing this photon fluid, we measure a dispersion relation that shows evidence of a single-particle region with parabolic characteristics along with linear acoustic modes. This holds true on our part, considering that interactions among the photon fluid may range and that sound speed can also remain relatively low or moderate under these conditions as observed. Furthermore with this analysis and experimental work done in this phase, static correlations in photon fluid states can also now be interpreted for various scenarios reported through quantum measurement interpretations reported through direct measurements.

Under uniform deformation, amorphous solids exhibit responses dominated by heterogeneous plastic instabilities arising from the localized, cooperative rearrangements of particle clusters; this behavior critically dictates their mechanical attributes. This paper utilizes computer simulations to investigate, within the context of simple shear in the athermal quasistatic limit, the properties and spatial relationships of clusters defined by non-affinite displacements in these solids. We observe that while large-mobility clusters are evenly distributed across the material before the elastic regime concludes, they localize into a shear band spanning the entire system post-yield displacement. Analysis reveals that displacement field distributions follow a power-law pattern where the exponents rely significantly on the specific deformation applied. Furthermore, significant spatial correlations exist in non-affinite displacements and extend to longer ranges as strain increases. Specifically, our findings indicate that correlation function decays are exponentially governed during the elastic phase. Once the material yields, this behavior abruptly switches; the subsequent correlations are adequately modeled as a power-law, demonstrating a scale-free signature for non-affinite clusters within the steady-flow condition. Crucially, these results remain consistent and are not influenced by the specific strain intervals chosen for calculating the aggregate non-affinite displacement.

Pair-wise loss functions facilitate metric learning by optimizing embeddings to ensure image representations from matching semantic categories are positioned closer together than those from distinct categories. While literature describes numerous evolving variations of this strategy, an analysis of the gradients of loss functions reveals components that dictate adjustments in relative feature placements for both anchor-positive and anchor-negative pairs. By examining these factors, researchers achieved a unified framework encompassing current variations, while revealing insights for a simplified algorithm; specifically by isolating pairs of gradient effects. Ultimately, constructing dedicated pairwise update mechanisms highlights key impacts and results in a state-of-the-art method that improves image search performance on the Stanford Online, CUB data repositories, as well as cars dataset (CAR).

Few-shot learning is an emerging approach designed for scenarios with limited data availability, aiming to classify previously unseen categories using only a small number of examples. Recent techniques, including metric learning, utilize meta-learning by structuring training into episodic tasks composed of support (-training) and query (test) data. These methods have proven that simple models can yield strong performance by learning a similarity metric to compare support and query instances. However, the feature space generated by specific metric learning strategies might not fully exploit task-specific signals. In this research, we investigate dimension reduction techniques to isolate features essential to the task, thereby enhancing predictive performance for few-shot classification in the reduced 空间。 We evaluate the reduced features by scoring based on intra- and inter-class distances and selecting methods that maximally enlarge inter-class distances while bringing instances within the same class closer together. By providing the metric learning similarity function with more discriminative input features, this process boosts classification accuracy. Our approach surpasses metric learning baselines on the miniImagenet dataset by achieving an accuracy gain of approximately 2 percentage points.

Single image-based crowd counting has become a highly prominent area of recent research owing to its extensive real-world applications. Numerous recent methodologies aim to solve the inherent challenges in crowd counting, relying principally on convolutional neural networks that demand vast training datasets to optimize network parameters. In response, we introduce "JHU-CROWD++," a new large-scale, unrestricted crowd counting collection comprising 4,372 images annotated with 1.51 million specific targets. Beyond surpassing other collections in scale, dataset images depict a spectrum of environments; they include weather-induced degradation and varying light conditions to ensure ultimate challenge for evaluative methods. The collection further offers comprehensive rich-level annotations, providing details at both image and individual head levels in addition to the standard annotations. We evaluated and benchmarked several latest approaches against this standard resource. The collection may be accessed for downloading at http://www.crowd-counting.com.

Beyond this, we have designed a unique crowd counting system that constructs group density images through progressive stages utilizing residual errors. The suggested approach adopts VGG16 as its framework while using density images produced in the ultimate depth layer as a rough estimate; this guide is refined through progressive stages that generate increasingly precise density images relying on residual techniques in turn. Moreover, these residual techniques follow an uncertainty driven confidence weighting strategy that limits the progression to high certainty residues in the optimization stages. The suggested Confidence Guided Deep Residual Counting Network (cg-drCN ) has been rigorously assessed across various complex datasets recently; it has achieved remarkable reductions in measurement errors.

Current methods for addressing dataset bias typically use a biased proxy model to flag biased instances, which are then down-weighted during main model training to improve robustness to out-of-distribution data. This strategy relies on the common assumption that the target model exhibits behaviors similar to the biased proxy machine, utilizing shortcuts only when possible. This paper challenges the universality of this premise. Through an exhaustive analysis of the MNLI and FEVER datasets using partial-input models and limited-capacity approaches for identifying biased instances, we demonstrate that the biased proxy model frequently fails to replicate the target model's predictions for one-third to half of the instances, primarily due to discrepancies in the specific input segments each model focuses on. Cohensive subgraph detection is a pivotal task in graphs, extensively utilized in fields like social community identification, topological analysis, and network visualization. While traditional cohesive measures often ensure strong structural properties, they are vulnerable to the free-rider phenomenon, where irrelevant clusters join a single subgraph merely by sharing a few edges or vertices. This paper focuses on $k$-vertex connected components (k-VCCs), a connectivity metric that is less commonly explored in the literature. A k-VCC is defined as a subgraph resilient to the removal of any $k-1$ vertices. Beyond mitigating the free-rider issue, k-VCCs offer benefits such as controlled diameters, superior cohesiveness, and limitations on overlapping graphs and subgraph counts. To address this problem efficiently, a polynomial-time algorithm has been introduced using a recursive approach to divide the input graph into an overlapped substructure. For a given simple undirected graph $G$, the independence complex $\mathrm{Ind}(G)$ is a simplicial complex constructed from independent vertex subsets, serving as an important intersection point among algebraic topology, commutative algebra, and graph theory. The collection of all such sets generates an simplicial complex denoted as the $r$-independence complex, $\mathrm{Ind}_r(G)$. It is established that for chordal graphs, $\mathrm{Ind}_r(G)$ possesses a wedge-of-spheres homotopy structure, prompting further investigation into conditions of shellability and, specifically, vertex decomposability for $G$ structured as graphs other than those where this holds trivially or naturally. We utilize Woodroofe's framework of chordal hypergraphs to demonstrate that for chordal graphs that are also trees, the complexes $\mathrm{In}_r(G)$ are invariably shellable. Moreover, by applying the concepts of vertex splittable ideals, we establish that for graphs shaped like caterpillars, the complexes $\mathrm{In}_r(G)$ achieve vertex decomposability across all integral values of $r$. Additionally, we present constructions of chordal graphs comprising exactly $2r+2$ vertices whose corresponding complexes fail to be sequentially Cohen-Macaulay for any $r\geq2$.

Segmenting labeled instances within unlabeled imaging modalities is a vital though difficult challenge, largely due to the costly and slow process of gathering expert annotations. Beyond incorporating CycleGAN losses for translation and supervised losses for the annotated source domain, our method integrates self-supervised and segmentation-driven adversarial objectives designed to boost performance by utilizing unlabeled images from the target domain. A core component of Active Learning (AL) revolves around determining which data should receive annotation. Experimental evaluations across classic image classification and semantic segmentation benchmarks, alongside a validation on cellular imaging—specifically cryo-Electron Tomography for subtomogram classification—showcase both the robustness to noise and domain utility of our approach. We introduce a novel strategy for optimizing quantum circuits grounded in ZX-calculus. First, we treat quantum circuits as ZX-diagrams, offering a adaptable, foundational graphical framework for expressing quantum calculations. Subsequently, we develop a reduction method using ZX-calculus rules, relying on two specific graph modifications: local complementation and pivoting. We demonstrate that the resulting streamlined diagram can be reversibly converted back into a circuit. Although converting general ZX-diagrams back into circuits remains understudied, we prove that our optimized diagrams inherently exhibit a graph property termed "flow," enabling a deterministic derivation process for the underlying circuits. In the context of Clifford circuits, this process identifies a novel standard format that achieves asymptotically minimal size while offering a refined upper limit for gate depth on near-edge systems. For broader circuit classes like Clifford+T and general circuits, this method effectively bypasses obstacles disrupting Clifford structures, resulting in compressed circuits compared to traditional "segment and redo" approaches.

LiDAR sensors play a crucial role in contemporary self-driving cars by delivering precise, high-definition 3D models of their surroundings. Nevertheless, effectively leveraging the growing volume of data from numerous high-fidelity LiDAR units poses significant computational hurdles. As sensor accuracy and point clouds increase in both spatial resolution and frame rates, maintaining real-time processing while extracting environmental semantics remains a critical challenge. This work analyzes the link between computational data representations and associated performance traits. Specifically, we introduce a novel categorization system for LiDAR point cloud formats within modern deep architectures. Leveraging this taxonomy, we systematically evaluate various method families, revealing shared strengths and bottlenecks regarding processing speed, memory consumption, and semantic capability—quantified through segmentation tasks. Lastly, our findings offer valuable direction for advancements in future neural processing of point clouds.

The neuro-fuzzy controller's parameter vectors are adaptively refined using the error surfaces generated by the SMC, creating an elastic structural framework wherein the quantity of fuzzy rules expands or contracts dynamically to optimize the bias-variance tradeoff. The study experimentally validates the controller's real-time interaction capabilities, specifically accounting for the ground effect, ceiling effect, time-based trajectory following, and flight through powerful fan-induced wind disturbances.

Since Davies points signify locations of infinite heat capacity, they typically mark second-order phase transitions in standard scaling; however, such transitions in these black holes fall into two categories: points representing extreme temperatures and those representing critical temperature inflection. Utilizing the generalized classification reveals a distinction: while the first category corresponds to a $3/2$-order transition and the second, critical type, to a $4/3$-order transition, this more precise framework can differentiate between transitions conventionally lumped together, thereby offering fresh perspectives into the thermodynamics of black holes.

Personalized gamification addresses the limitations of a single solution by leveraging user knowledge to create customized designs. This tailoring process integrates both user profiles and contextual factors—such as specific activities and geographical locations—to generate opportunities for adaptation across multiple levels, necessitating automated tools for personalization. Current challenges include determining which characteristics are most influential and identifying methods for implementation, while a scarcity of suitable automated systems remains. This project addresses these issues in two phases: first, an explorary survey gathered user preferences on which gamification elements are most beneficial for different learning activity types (LATs), followed by the creation of a conditional decision tree model based on the survey results to inform the tailoring process. Second, this model was translated into a practical product—a recommender system capable of automatically suggesting personalized gamification strategies. Our findings confirm (i) that users' preferences are shaped by learning activities, geography, and various other attributes, (ii) that gamification can be designed with simultaneous consideration for both user and contextual data, and (iii) that technological solutions exist to aid such design processes. Ultimately, the key takeaway for defining gamification strategies involves considering a combination of demographics, game mechanics, geography, learning activities, and the interplay between these factors, while utilizing our recommender system as an effective support tool for personalization.

Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) transform inputs through a set of human-interpretable concepts known as a bottleneck and generate subsequent predictions leveraging this structure. Detecting and eliminating suspected hostile nodes in connected systems is critical. However, the inherent uncertainty in identification processes, when combined with network topology, imposes indirect costs associated with either accidentally removing legitimate nodes or missing malicious ones. Although a recent method was developed to specifically address these challenges, it relies significantly on a limiting assumption: that the decision maker perfectly understands the joint probability of node malignancy across the network. Practically, such perfect knowledge is unattainable, as the underlying distribution is usually only an approximation derived from limited data points. Consequently, we introduce a framework for robust distribution handling designed to ensure optimal node elimination despite these uncertainties. Fear of depredation, a non-consumptive effect, significantly shapes predator-prey interactions, a phenomenon less explored in purely competitive contexts given the relevant ecological and social motivations. Recently, reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated significant promise for addressing tasks in structured domains such as games and robotics. This study focuses on solving a robotic reaching task within a simulation using the Neurorobotics Platform (NRP). The target location is set randomly at the start, requiring a 6-degree-of-freedom robot to move in a single continuous trajectory. Following this baseline, we escalate the scenario's difficulty by employing visual inputs derived from the simulated environment to inform agent actions. Our experimental data indicates that an effective training performance is achievable by applying a suitable dynamic schedule function for implementing curriculum learning.

Detecting and addressing overconfidence when deep neural networks encounter out-of-distribution (OOD) samples remains a challenging problem. The proposed solution inherently relies on creating a subset of OOD data specifically designed to suppress model confidence, rather than eliminating them. This study introduces Chamfer OOD examples (CODEs)—synthetic data points with distributions resembling in-distribution samples—that effectively mitigate OOD overconfidence through targeted prediction suppression. We generate CODEs first using "slices-and-splices" techniques applied to in-distributions across various classes to produce seed OOD samples; these seeds are subsequently transformed into the desired close-to-in-distributions via an unsupervised Chamfer-based Generative Adversarial Network without needing external datasets. Experimental validation shows that training while suppressing predictions on CODEs substantially reduces OOD overconfidence without degrading overall classification precision, outperforming existing state-of-the-art approaches, while also serving as a beneficial resource for OOD detection.

Identifying the most pivotal or ranking vertices in directed and undirected graphs is a fundamental task in graph-based applications, a goal typically addressed through various centrality measures defined in literature. By analyzing a graph's structural properties, these methods evaluate relative node importance, while a recently introduced family specifically suited for graph databases relies on the concept that a node's significance corresponds to the count of surrounding "relevant" connected structures, termed subgraph motifs. Consequently, their members are classified as "subgraph motif centrality measures." Although existing research confirms these measures posit beneficial characteristics, their ultimate expressiveness has largely remained undefined. The primary aim of this work is to rigorously characterize the absolute expressiveness of this measure family across both undirected and directed contexts. Specifically, we determine when arbitrary measures belong to the subgraph motif class relative to either the measure itself or the resulting rankings. Furthermore, we establish whether established centrality measures fall into this family using derived tools that facilitate such classification. Beyond intrinsic theoretical value, categorizing well-known metrics in this manner offers valuable insights regarding the core structural similarities and distinctions existing between different centrality approaches.

Achievable prediction uncertainty estimation represents a crucial prerequisite for reliably deploying deep object detectors in safety-critical applications. This study focuses on predicting full distributions for bounding box regression using variance-modulated architectures. We demonstrate that, despite the potential for high accuracy in predicted mean locations, training variance networks via negative log likelihood (NLL) can result in overly dispersed, high-entropy predictions regardless of their actual quality. Instead, we propose employing an Energy score as a non-local and proper scoring rule; our experiments indicate that optimizing this metric yields significantly better calibrated results with lower uncertainty compared to standard NLL training. Furthermore, we critique the prevalent use of non-proper metrics for evaluating probabilistic outputs in object detection and introduce an alternative assessment framework based strictly on proper scoring rules. Leveraging these new tools, we reveal that while variance networks generate meaningful distributions, current heuristic methods used in foundational object detection literature for setting regression targets provide insufficient data support for robust uncertainty learning. Ultimately, our contributions aim to align evaluation practices for probabilistic detection with established uncertainty evaluation methods in broader machine learning fields. The code underlying our models, datasets, and evaluation procedures is hosted at: https://github.com/asharakeh/probdet.git.
